activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Charles David Keeling of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958; the resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.
story:
The trail switchbacked up through pines that smelled like rain even though the sky was clear, and Madeline kept her thumb on the notes app the whole climb, scrolling the same half-finished paragraph again and again. Her presentation was Monday. It was Saturday. Somewhere in her draft was a graph she had drawn on graph paper at one in the morning, a line jagging up like a stuttering staircase, and beneath it a caption that read, in her own handwriting, "Data from, uh."

"You're going to walk off the edge of the world doing that," Shiloh said, catching Madeline's elbow and steering her around a root. "The trail. The cliff. The drop."

"The greenhouse effect," Madeline said. "That's what you're worried about me falling into?"

Shiloh laughed. Muhammad, a few steps behind with the water bottles, said, "Explain it to us, then. We're a captive audience. If you can teach it to us on a hill, you can teach it to a classroom."

So she tried, between switchbacks, with her hands: sunlight comes in, passes right through the air the way light passes through a window, and warms the ground. The ground sends heat back up, but that heat is a different thing, and some of the gases in the air, carbon dioxide among them, hold onto it. The window lets the light in and doesn't let the warmth out. "It's not a conspiracy," she said. "It's plumbing. It's just the way the molecules are."

"Okay," Muhammad said. "So then why does anyone argue about it?"

"Because the graph," Madeline said, and stopped. The wind moved through the pines above them and she watched the tops of the trees bend all together, like a crowd leaning toward something. "There's this graph. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured continuously for over sixty years. It goes up. And up. It wiggles every year, up and down, like breathing, but the whole thing climbs. Everyone in the world has seen it. And I put it in my slides and I wrote the caption and then I realized I don't actually know where the measurements come from. Who took them. Where. I've been staring at the picture for two days and I never once asked whose instrument it is."

Her phone had no bars. She had known that, in some part of her mind, since the parking lot, and she had been carrying the phone up the mountain anyway, the way you carry a flashlight in daylight.

They reached a granite overlook where Ms. Cho was already waiting, sitting on a flat boulder with a thermos, because she had agreed to drive them and then refused to sit in the car for three hours. Ms. Cho taught chemistry at the school, though Madeline had never had her, and Madeline had been careful, all morning, not to ask her anything. It felt like cheating. It felt, more precisely, like the difference between knowing a thing and knowing where it came from, and Madeline had only just discovered that difference existed, and it embarrassed her.

"Present it to me," Ms. Cho said now, without being asked, as though she had followed the whole climb by listening to its silences. "Half of it. The half you're sure of."

Madeline did the window and the molecules again, slower, better. Ms. Cho nodded once. "And the graph?"

"I can tell you what it looks like," Madeline said. "I can tell you it wiggles and climbs. I can't tell you who made it, and I have to be able to, because otherwise I'm just holding up a picture and saying trust me, and I don't want to be the kind of person who does that." She heard herself and flushed. Shiloh looked at the horizon. Muhammad studied his shoes.

Ms. Cho poured coffee and did not volunteer anything, which Madeline understood, later, was the entire lesson of the morning. There was a long quiet in which the sun came fully over the ridge and the valley below turned from grey to green, the mist off the creek gone evanescent, dissolving even as Madeline watched it. Then Ms. Cho said, "There's a plaque at the visitor center, down at the trailhead. I read it while I waited for you three to finish arguing about snacks."

They came off the mountain faster than they went up. At the visitor center, a low brown building with humming vending machines, Madeline found the plaque between a case of pinned butterflies and a map of the watershed. She stood in front of it and read it twice. Charles David Keeling, of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in March 1958. The resulting graph is called the Keeling Curve.

"Mauna Loa," she said out loud, tasting it. "It's a volcano. He picked a volcano."

"Why?" Muhammad asked.

She shook her head. "The plaque doesn't say. I'll find out before Monday." She took out her phone, and this time the bars were back, and she typed the name into her notes before she could lose it, caption rewritten in her head already: Data from Mauna Loa Observatory, begun 1958. Then she looked up the trail she had just climbed, grey thread stitched onto the mountain, and thought about the little station standing above the clouds in Hawaii, taking its measurement tonight, the same as every night since before her parents were born.

"Presentation's Monday," Shiloh said. "Want to come over tomorrow and draw the graph big?"

"Bring the graph paper," Madeline said. "And more ink."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
story:
The resolution on the board read that the state should fund a universal basic income, and Jasmine had argued both sides of it so many times in practice that she sometimes forgot which one she believed. That was supposed to be a strength. Mr. Sok said the best debaters could hold a position like water in cupped hands, but this afternoon, in the actual semifinal against Halloway Prep, her hands felt full of holes. She stood at the podium for her rebuttal with two index cards and a silence that stretched two seconds too long.

Halloway's second speaker, a boy with a faintly bored voice, had just run a syllogism at her. If poverty causes crime, and if this city has poverty, then this city has crime. Therefore, he'd said, leaning into the therefore, the affirmative's plan addresses the root cause of crime, which the negative has conceded matters. It sounded airtight. It sounded like a trap door opening under her feet, and she had hesitated, which in debate is a kind of confession.

"All right," she said finally, and heard her own voice steady itself. "Let's talk about the form of my opponent's argument." She looked down at her cards, then put them face down on the ledge, a gesture she'd stolen from Olivia, who argued best when she appeared to be arguing from nothing. "He says: if poverty causes crime, and this city has poverty, then this city has crime. Notice what he hasn't shown us. He hasn't shown that poverty causes crime. He's asked you to accept the shape of the argument instead of its substance."

From the third row, Leena mouthed something at her, too fast to read. Leena had drilled her on this for two weeks after the coffee shop, the afternoon that had started the whole thing. It had begun with dragons, of all things. Olivia had declared, over a table littered with cups, that all dragons breathe fire, and Jasmine breathes fire, therefore Jasmine is a dragon. Leena had laughed and said the argument was obviously nonsense because dragons didn't exist. Olivia had refused to budge. It's valid, she'd kept saying, jabbing her straw at Jasmine like a pointer. Valid doesn't mean true. An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. Validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true. Jasmine had walked home that night turning the sentence over, feeling that something important had been handed to her in a paper bag.

"That's a claim about validity," she said now, and the word sat in the room like a coin dropped on a table. "Validity depends only on the form, not on whether the premises are true. So my opponent can build a perfectly valid argument on a premise that's false. He probably has. But I want to be fair to him, so let's do what he's asking, and test the premise itself." She pulled a statistic from memory, one she'd found at one in the morning and half doubted: the counterexample city, where poverty had fallen over ten years and crime had not moved. "Conditional thinking cuts both ways," she said. "If he gets to say if poverty causes crime, I get to ask what happens when we find a place where it didn't."

The Halloway boy's face did something small during her second point, a tightening around the mouth that she catalogued without pity. He had built a beautiful machine and she was pointing out that no one had plugged it in. It occurred to her, mid-sentence, that this was also a way of prevaricating, a more respectable kind, because she had not actually said whether she thought the plan would work. She had said the argument failed, not that the policy did, and the judges might not notice the gap she'd left, and she had chosen to leave it.

Mr. Sok was timing her from the back, one hand on the stopwatch, and she remembered him at practice in October, telling her she prevaricated when she was cornered, and her protesting that debate was performance, that everyone shaded things. He hadn't argued. He'd just waited, the way he did, until she heard herself. The historiography unit he'd taught that fall had unsettled her the same way, the discovery that historians disagreed not because some were liars but because the questions they asked shaped the answers they found. Two people could look at the same century and come out with different centuries.

She used her last thirty seconds to concede something, which was her hedge and her habit, an ancillary move she'd learned from Leena, who called it "giving them a hand so they don't notice you've taken the arm." "Maybe the plan does reduce poverty," she said. "I don't know. I'm telling you the affirmative hasn't shown it tonight, and a conclusion that hasn't been shown isn't a conclusion you can vote on." She sat down. Leena was already scribbling on the flow sheet, drawing arrows from her rebuttal to the final speech, mapping the round like a battle.

The twist came in cross-examination, when the Halloway boy stood to question her and did not ask about poverty at all. "Your counterexample city," he said. "Where did you get it?" She told him: a longitudinal study, the kind with tables in the appendix. He nodded, almost gently. "Because I pulled that study last night too. Their crime figures were undercounted. The authors issued a correction in March." The room went very quiet, the particular quiet of an audience realizing it is watching something private. Jasmine felt the floor of her own argument open, and beneath it another floor, and beneath that nothing she could name.

She could have stonewalled. She could have demanded he produce the correction, could have made him prove a thing she suddenly half-suspected was true. Instead she heard herself say, "Then my counterexample fails, and that part of my rebuttal fails with it." She kept her eyes on him while she said it, and noticed, absurdly, that he looked almost disappointed, as though he'd wanted a fight and been handed a receipt. "But the validity point stands," she added. "A sound premise doesn't rescue an argument that was never shown to be valid in the first place, and neither of us showed that tonight. We built two machines and neither of us turned either one on."

When the judges retired, Leena leaned over the flow sheet and asked her, quietly, whether she'd just lost the round to win an argument. Jasmine looked at the resolution on the board, at the two empty podiums, at Mr. Sok's stopwatch face going dark. "I don't know yet," she said. "Ask me which one I was trying to do."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area between two curves is found by integrating the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they are ordered that way.
story:
Christian's mother had pushed the kitchen table against the wall so the math club could fit, and by seven o'clock there were five of them around it, three textbooks, and a plate of biscuits nobody touched because they were all arguing. Fares had his calculator flat on the table like evidence in a trial. Jacob had his notebook open to a page torn halfway down.

"Twenty-seven over six," Fares said. "I did it twice."

"Negative twenty-seven over six," Jacob said. "Also twice."

Ms. Kamau, who lived two doors down and had agreed to supervise only if nobody made her supervise, was reading a novel by the window and pretending not to listen. Christian looked from one notebook to the other. The problem was on the whiteboard his father had mounted above the toaster: find the area between the line and the parabola between their two crossing points. Same interval. Same curves. Two answers, one of them negative, which everyone knew area could not be.

"You subtracted wrong," Fares said. "You did the parabola minus the line."

"So did you do the line minus the parabola?" Jacob asked. "Who decided your order is the right one?"

The question was fair, Christian thought, and it was the first thing anyone had said all evening that actually interested him. At school, getting a negative area was the kind of mistake that could stigmatize you in a class like theirs, where people filed each other's competence away in the first week of September and rarely updated the file. Jacob had already been filed. Christian watched him hunch slightly over his notebook, braced for the verdict, and felt a somatic flicker of that old fear in himself, the tightness across the shoulders that had come with every wrong answer since grade four.

He picked up the marker. "Where do they cross?" he asked.

Fares, who had memorized the algebra, said the values immediately, and Christian marked both points on the sketch of the parabola, then drew the line cutting through it. Between the crossings, the parabola sat below the line. It was obvious once drawn, the way things were. The region between them was a lens shape, and the line was its ceiling.

"So over that whole interval," Christian said slowly, "the line is the upper one. The area between two curves is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function, over the interval where they're ordered that way." He heard himself say it and checked it against the picture. Upper minus lower. Line minus parabola. That gave Fares's answer, positive, and it gave it not because Fares had friends in higher places but because of the geometry, which did not care about either of them.

"Then my subtraction was backwards," Jacob said.

"Your subtraction was the only thing wrong," Christian said. "The setup, the limits, all of it was right."

Jacob looked at the board for a moment. "You're not just saying that."

"He's not just saying that," Fares said, and pushed the biscuits toward him.

Christian sat down and worked the integral himself, top to bottom, and got the same number, and understood, in the modest way understanding arrived, that he had not known this an hour ago. He had spent the autumn treating calculus as a set of procedures to be executed before anyone noticed he was executing them slowly. The difference between procedure and reason had never been clearer than it was tonight: Jacob had followed every procedure and arrived at a negative area, a quantity the physical world refused to contain, and the reason, the ordering of the curves, was the thing that saved you from that.

He was honest with himself about what he still did not know. He could see that the ordering held over the whole interval this time, but he wondered what happened with curves that crossed in the middle, whether the upper function could change identity partway through, and whether the rule he had just spoken aloud would need him to break the interval into pieces. He wrote the question in the margin of his notebook without answering it.

Ms. Kamau turned a page. "For a woman who isn't supervising," she said, not looking up, "I'll just mention that this is the quietest argument I've heard in years, and I used to mark provincial exams."

Fares grinned. Jacob was already reworking his solution, pen moving fast, and when he finished he looked up at Christian with an expression that seemed to question its own veracity, as if a correct answer from his own hand needed independent confirmation before it could be believed.

"Twenty-seven over six," Jacob said.

"Twenty-seven over six," Christian said, and capped the marker.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
David had the books spread across the kitchen table in a fan, three of them from the library and two from Mr. Sinclair's classroom shelf, and none of them agreed. The prompt sat beside his elbow: how have views of the French Revolution changed since 1800. He had been at the table since four, and it was now past seven, and the essay existed so far as one sentence in his notebook, crossed out.

"You're still on that?" Vince stood in the doorway with his jacket still on, holding a basketball under one arm. "We're meeting Trevor at the courts at eight."

"I can't. I don't have anything yet."

Vince dropped the ball on a chair and leaned over the table. He read the prompt out loud, slowly, the way he read anything. "Since 1800. That's like two hundred years of people arguing."

"That's the point. That's the whole assignment." David turned one of the books around so Vince could see the chapter heading, then turned it back. "It's not about the Revolution. It's about the historians."

"So write that Marx ruined everything and move on."

"That's not even close to how it works." David said it more sharply than he meant to. He was thinking of the paragraph he'd drafted that afternoon, the one that had collapsed when he tried to predicate the whole essay on the claim that historians had simply inherited a Marxist story without questioning it. He had no evidence. He had a feeling, and Mr. Sinclair had told them in September that feelings were not historiography.

Vince spun the ball on one finger, watched it wobble, caught it. "So what's the problem, exactly?"

"I need the moment. Where somebody actually pushed back. Not a footnote. A real challenge, with a name on it."

"Trevor's brother did this essay last year," Vince said. "He said he just wrote about Napoleon the whole time."

"He failed, then, or he should have." David pulled the notebook toward himself again. He had written and crossed out a date, 1800, then a question mark, then nothing. The library books treated the Marxist interpretation the way weather treats the sky, as simply the condition things happened in. One of them, a thick survey with a cracked spine, had a chapter called "Revisionism" that he had skimmed standing up in the stacks. He found it now and put his finger on the page.

"There," he said, almost to himself.

Vince came around the table. "There what?"

"Alfred Cobban. His inaugural lecture at University College London, 1954." David ran his finger down the paragraph. "Published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. It attacked the Marxist social interpretation. That's the moment. That's where it turns."

"Attacked it how?"

David read further, lips moving. "That's the part I can't get into, not really. He went after the idea that it was a bourgeois revolution, that a rising class overthrew a feudal one. But people had already started chipping at it before him, and I can't tell how much of the turn was him and how much was attrition, everyone grinding away at the same wall for years." He looked up. "I think I have to say that. That I can't entirely tell."

"That sounds like a C."

"That sounds like an honest paragraph." David heard his own voice and wondered if it was stubbornness talking. He had watched Trevor, in their seminar on Thursday, deliver a confident five minutes on how the Revolution had been "about class, obviously," and Mr. Sinclair had said nothing, had only written something in his binder, and the silence had been worse than an argument. Mercurial, Trevor had called the Revolution afterward, as if the word settled it, as if a thing could be both storm and explanation.

Vince set the ball down on the table, on top of the crossed-out sentence. "So you can come shoot for forty minutes and still be back by nine."

"No."

"You're no fun when you're like this."

"You can go. Seriously." David was already flipping to a blank page. "Tell Trevor I owe him one."

Vince stood there a second longer, then picked up the ball and let himself out. The door clicked. The kitchen went quiet enough that David could hear the refrigerator, and upstairs a parent's footsteps crossing some other room, unhurried, uninterested in 1789 or 1954.

He wrote: The Marxist interpretation did not fall in a single afternoon, but Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, marked the point at which the challenge could no longer be ignored. He looked at it. It was one sentence out of perhaps twenty he would need, and he could already see the seams where he would have to admit what stayed uncertain. Outside, a car door slammed, and somewhere down the block Vince's voice rose and broke into laughter. David turned the page and kept writing.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: 'Ibid.' abbreviates the Latin 'ibidem', meaning 'in the same place', and is used in a note citing the same source as the note just before it.
story:
The library smelled of warm toner and somebody's microwave noodles, and Caleb had been staring at the same photocopied page for eleven minutes. It was a model research paper Mr. Dlamini had handed out, five pages about a court case in which a student had sued a school after being hurt in gym class, and down the bottom of page three the footnotes turned strange. The first one was long, a full citation with a title and page numbers. The next three said only a single word: Ibid. Ibid. Ibid. He turned the page. Another one. He looked up at Phoenix, who was across the table with her own copy, chewing the cap of a highlighter.

"Do you know what this means?" Caleb asked, tapping the word. "It just says Ibid, over and over."

Phoenix leaned over, reading upside down with the ease of someone who had done it all her life. "No idea. Maybe it's a typo. Maybe the printer ran out of words."

Royce dropped into the chair beside her, late as always, his backpack half unzipped and exhaling papers. "The printer ran out of words," he repeated, in the querulous tone he used when he thought everyone else was having more fun than him. "You two get to be funny. I got a topic I can't stand." His assignment sheet, flattened on the table, said his paper had to make an argument, not just report facts, and his argument was supposed to be about whether the school could make athletes sign a waiver that promised to indemnify the district, to cover its costs, if the athlete got hurt. He had underlined the word four times in the handout like stabbing it.

"That's your problem, not mine," Phoenix said. "My problem is I found twelve sources and they all disagree and I don't know who's right."

"That's not a problem," Caleb said. "That's the whole assignment." He said it before he'd decided to, and it came out more certain than he felt. He slid the model paper toward the middle of the table. "Look, this is the paper Mr. Dlamini got an A on, whoever wrote it. It argues that the waiver the kid signed shouldn't have stopped the lawsuit. And the footnotes go like this." He pointed. "Full citation, then Ibid, then Ibid, then Ibid, then a new full citation, then Ibid again. So the Ibo one comes right after a different full one."

Phoenix took the highlighter cap out of her mouth. "So it's short for something."

"It's short for ibidem," Royce said. They both looked at him. He shrugged, reddening. "It's Latin. It means in the same place. My dad's a lawyer, I've read enough legal paper to last a lifetime. Deposition transcripts use it too, sometimes, the old ones." He pulled the model paper closer, annoyed at himself for knowing things. "So Ibid means you're citing the same source as the note just before it. Same book, same place."

Caleb sat back. The page rearranged itself in his head, the way a puzzle does when one piece drops in. The four Ibo notes all pointed back to that first long citation, the court opinion, and the writer was using the same opinion again and again because that was where the argument actually lived. "So it's not laziness," he said. "It's a way of saying, I'm still here, I'm still drawing from this. It keeps the argument honest without repeating everything."

"It could also be a way of hiding that you only read one source," Phoenix said. She had her chin in her hand, watching the footnotes like they might move. "My twelve sources disagreeing might be better than this guy's one source repeated."

"Or worse," Caleb said. "Twelve sources and no argument is just noise." He heard himself and slowed down. "I don't actually know which it is. Maybe you need the one source you trust and then a couple to push against it." He pulled a blank sheet toward him and started a bibliography page, handwriting the first entry, then stopped. "Wait. If I cite the same article twice in a row, I get to use it." He wrote the word in the margin, small, to try it. Ibid. It looked like a password.

Royce had gone quiet, reading the model paper's argument about the waiver. His finger stopped on a line where the writer admitted the courts in one state had gone the other way and the student had lost. "This guy put the part that wrecks his case right in the middle," Royce said. "That's weird. Isn't that like scoring for the other team?"

"Or it's like saying you're not lying," Caleb said.

Phoenix uncapped her highlighter and drew a green box around all four Ibo notes at once, one stroke. "Fine. I'll keep six of my sources and pick a fight between two of them and drop the rest. But if Mr. Dlamini marks me down for too few sources, I'm telling him it was your theory."

The library lights buzzed and dimmed for a second, the way they did every afternoon around three. Caleb looked down at his blank page, then at the model, then wrote his first footnote the slow way, every part of it, author and title and page, because you had to give the full thing once before you could earn the short word. Royce picked up his pen, crossed out the title of his paper, and wrote a new one underneath: The Waiver That Promised Too Much. Phoenix read it upside down and nodded. "Better," she said, and Caleb underlined his footnote twice and started the second one, writing Ibid.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Ricardo's original model treats labor as the only cost of production and assumes that cost stays the same however much of a good is made.
story:
Riley had claimed the corner table by the pretzel stand at half past two on a Saturday, which was either diligence or defeat, since the essay was due Monday and he had forty dollars riding on finishing something else first. The something else was Pierce, who slid into the seat across from him with a twenty in his fist and the expression of a boy purchasing absolution.

"Explain comparative advantage," Pierce said. "The whole thing. Ms. Nowak says if I bomb the econ section she's calling home, and my dad already bought the plane ticket for the graduation trip, so."

"So this is where the plane ticket gets underwritten," Riley said, and took the twenty, because eighteen is old enough to have principles but not so old that they survive contact with cash. The food court smelled of cinnamon and floor cleaner. Somewhere behind them a toddler was losing a war with an ice cream cone.

Riley lined up salt packets and napkins on the table. "Okay. Say this napkin's Portugal and it makes wine. This one's England and it makes cloth. Portugal's better at both. Better at wine, better at cloth. And they still both get richer if they trade."

"That's the part that sounds fake," Pierce said.

"It sounds fake because you're thinking about it wrong." Riley slid the packets around, using long ones for wine and torn ones for cloth, and he made Pierce compute how many napkins each country gave up to make one more packet, and watched the exact moment Pierce's face changed, the little collapse of a person watching arithmetic beat intuition. "Portugal gives up less cloth to get wine than England does. So even though Portugal's better at everything, it's least-better at cloth, comparatively, and England is least-worse at cloth. Each one does the thing it's comparatively good at, they trade, both come out ahead. That's the whole trick."

"Write that down," Pierce said, with the reverence of a man dictating to a stenographer, and Riley wrote it down, and then Pierce said the fatal thing, which was, "So is it true? Like, actually?"

Riley stopped with the pen in the air. Because the honest answer was that he had never asked. He'd absorbed the model the way you absorb a magic trick, admiring the mechanism without wondering what the magician's sleeve was made of. He looked at his salt packets, arranged in their tidy two-country world, and asked himself what the packets were pretending not to have. Wages? Machines? The rent on the vineyard?

"Labor," he said slowly. "It's all labor. Ricardo counts labor as the only cost of production. The cloth costs however many hours of work, the wine costs hours. Nothing else exists."

"So no machines."

"No machines, no materials, no rent. Hours and hours and nothing but hours." Riley felt something loosen in his understanding, the way a knot you've been gripping turns out to have a slack end. "And here's the other thing. The hours stay the same however much you make. The first packet costs the same as the ten-thousandth. He just assumes that."

"Is that true in real life?"

"I don't know yet. That's probably the point of asking." Riley flipped to a fresh page and began listing the assumptions in plain sentences, because you couldn't criticize a building until you knew which walls were load-bearing. Labor only. Constant costs. Two countries, two goods, no transport, no tariffs. The list had a clean, almost naive geometry to it, like a model of a bridge made of drinking straws.

"Trace," Pierce called, without turning around, because Trace had materialized from the pretzel stand with a tray, her break apparently timed by sonar. She set down three sodas and looked at the wreckage of napkins and salt.

"Homework on a Saturday," she said. "In a mall. You two are a cautionary exhibit."

"Riley's getting paid," Pierce said.

"Riley's getting robbed." She dropped into the third chair, which was the chair of someone who wanted to be part of whatever this was, and Riley suspected she'd been watching them for twenty minutes out of pure boredom, her nascent interest in their table having finally overtaken her obligation to the register. She peered at his list. "My econ teacher did this exact example. She said the constant costs part is the first thing that breaks, because in real factories the cost doesn't stay the same, it bends."

"That's what I wrote," Riley said, which was a subterfuge so immediate and so transparent that he regretted it before the last syllable landed. What he had written was "check whether costs bend."

Trace read the page anyway. "You didn't write that. You wrote 'check.'"

"That's called research."

"That's called not knowing yet," she said, and Pierce laughed into his soda, and Riley found he didn't mind, because the strange thing about admitting the gap was that the model got bigger on the other side of it. The straw bridge couldn't carry real trains, sure. But now he could see why someone had built it out of straws, and what you'd need to add to carry freight, and that was more interesting than the trick had been.

Pierce copied Riley's pages into his own notebook in slow, careful letters, like a man transcribing a pardon. He paused at the assumptions list. "So when Ms. Nowak asks if trade is always good, I say?"

"You say the model says both countries gain, and then you say the model assumes labor is the only cost and the cost stays the same however much you make, and then you say whether you buy it," Riley said. "The last part's yours. I can't sell you that for twenty."

Pierce looked at the page for a long moment. "Could do thirty."

Trace stole one of his fries.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States.
story:
The archive kept its lights low, as if brightness might damage the past, and Lucas found a table near the microfilm readers where he could spread both books without meeting anyone's eyes. One was by a historian who argued the Cold War was chiefly an American overreaction, paranoia institutionalized; the other, by a historian who treated Soviet espionage as a real and shaping force. Mr. Foster had assigned him a simple, impossible task: decide which explanation the evidence supports, and be ready to say why on Monday.

The trouble was that both writers sounded right. The first had a gift for the telling detail, the memorandum that revealed a general's fear more plainly than any policy paper. The second moved in broader strokes but kept pointing at names, at networks, at things the first writer dismissed as invention. Lucas had been reading for two hours and had filled a legal pad with page references that contradicted each other in ways he could not straighten out.

Savana dropped into the chair across from him with her own stack of folders, her library card held between her teeth while she pulled off her jacket. She glanced at his pad, then at the books, then back at him. "You look like somebody incapacitated you with a legal pad," she said. "Which one is winning?"

"Neither. That's the problem." He turned one of the books around so she could see the copyright page. "Look at when this was published."

She leaned in. "Nineteen eighty-eight."

"And the other one, two thousand four." He said it flatly, because he had only just understood what it meant, and he wanted to hear whether it sounded as significant aloud as it had in his head. "The newer book talks about the Venona decrypts. The older one couldn't."

Edison arrived late, breathless, holding a photocopy he had clearly paid for at the desk. "You have to see this," he said, sitting down without being asked. "The Venona decrypts of Soviet intelligence messages, released by the US government in 1995, confirmed that Soviet spy networks had operated in the United States. It's right there in the finding aid." He slid the page between their folders. "The archivist pulled it for me when I asked what came in that year."

Lucas read the sentence twice. It was not a long sentence, and it was not a dramatic one, but it rearranged something in his thinking the way a key rearranges a lock. The older historian had not ignored the espionage; he had written before anyone could read the decrypted messages, before the confirmation existed. His account was not dishonest. It was written in a different state of knowledge, the way a map drawn before a coast is surveyed is not a lie about the coast.

"So the newer guy wins," Savana said.

"That's what I thought for about a minute." Lucas pulled the legal pad toward him and found the page where he had copied out a passage from the first book, a passage about fear and its consequences, about how a nation that believed itself threatened could damage itself in ways no enemy could manage. "But knowing the networks were real doesn't tell you the fear was proportionate. It doesn't tell you how much of the Cold War those networks explain and how much is something else. The decrypts are one weight on the scale. They don't settle where it tips."

They worked until the lights above the main hall dimmed for closing, Edison photocopying the finding aid, Savana organizing her own folders, Lucas writing a page that began with the publication dates and ended with a question he could not make into a statement. His position, if he could call it that, was that the second historian's evidence was stronger, and that the first historian's way of thinking still accounted for something the evidence alone left turbid and unexplained, and that he would stand up on Monday and admit the middle of it was uncertain. The three of them packed up in the blue half-dark, and at the door the archivist held it open and nodded at the photocopy sticking out of Edison's bag.

"Careful with that," she said. "It's heavier than it looks."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
story:
Jack had agreed to explain DNA to Vince in exchange for three hours of volunteering at the community garden, which was a trade he was already regretting, because Vince kept wandering off to look at the bees. The deal had been brokered by Mr. Leung, who ran the garden and who taught nothing, officially, but who had a way of standing beside a person until a reasonable arrangement suggested itself. Jack needed the hours for his scholarship application. Vince needed to pass the biology retest on Monday. Neither of them had anticipated that the pea rows would become a classroom.

"Start with the copying part," Vince said, kneeling in the dirt with the textbook balanced on a watering can. "Transcription. Say it like I'm five."

"You're sixteen," Jack said, but he crouched down anyway. He drew a ladder in the dust with a stick, then unzipped it with his finger. DNA unzips, he said, and a copy gets made, a single strand called mRNA, and that copy travels out of the nucleus to where the protein gets built. Then translation: the mRNA gets read three letters at a time, and every three-letter word, every codon, calls for one amino acid, and the amino acids get clicked together in order. That's the protein.

"So the DNA is like a recipe," Vince said, "and the protein is like the cake."

"That's actually decent," Jack admitted, and Vince looked so pleased that Jack decided not to mention that the cake could be anything from a toenail to a brain chemical.

Mr. Leung came past with a tray of seedlings and paused, listening, the way he did. "In my day we called it the central dogma," he said, "though I never liked the word dogma. It sounds like arguing with it is against the rules."

The trouble started with the textbook's problem set, question four, which Jack had brought in his backpack. They worked it at the picnic table by the littoral bed of grasses Mr. Leung had planted along the drainage ditch, where the soil stayed damp and the mosquitoes gathered like a small determined congregation. The question gave a stretch of DNA, then the same stretch with one letter changed, and asked what would happen to the protein. Jack worked the first one out, reading codons off the chart, translating letter by letter. Then he did the second one and got, letter for letter, exactly the same amino acids. The changed DNA spelled the same protein.

"That can't be right," Vince said. "A mutation is supposed to do something. Mess something up. That's the whole drama of mutations."

Jack checked it twice. His stick tapped each codon in the dust, three letters, three letters, and each time the chart gave the same amino acid as before. A different word, the same meaning. He thought of his mother, who said "sofa" and "couch" interchangeably and meant the same nap on either one. He thought, for no good reason, of determinism, which they'd argued about in philosophy club, whether everything was fated down to the letter, and here was a letter changing and fate not caring at all.

"We should ask Mr. Leung," Vince said.

"He grows tomatoes. He's not going to know."

"He called it the central dogma unprompted. The man is hiding depths."

Mr. Leung was staking beans, and he listened to their problem without staking anything for a full minute, which Jack understood as a good sign. Then he said, "Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein." He handed Jack a bean pole as if it were punctuation. "They're called silent mutations," he said, and went back to his beans.

Vince turned to Jack with the expression of a boy who had been handed a cheat code. "Silent. Like the mutation happens and nobody even sends a card."

"So it's not that nothing happened," Jack said slowly, working it through aloud because that was the only way he ever worked anything through. "The DNA changed. The RNA changed. The codon is a different word. It just doesn't change the meaning." He paused. "I was going to teach you this. I had a whole plan with the seed packets."

"Your plan didn't have silent mutations in it."

"My plan was twenty minutes long. We've been here two hours."

Hugo arrived then, late and unapologetic, carrying the lemonade he'd been sent for an hour earlier, most of it drunk. He remonstrated with the mosquitoes, then with the textbook, then sat down and demanded to know why they looked like people who had seen something profound in a bean row. When Jack explained it, the changed letter and the unchanged protein, Hugo frowned and said it bothered him, that a code you could alter without consequence seemed sloppy, like a language with too many synonyms. Vince said it seemed merciful, like the universe letting you off with a warning. Jack found he couldn't pick a side, exactly. He liked both ideas, and he suspected the truth was that the system was neither careful nor careless, only old and elaborate and full of slack in its ropes.

He copied question four into his notebook and drew a small asterisk beside it, which stood for everything he hadn't figured out yet. "Monday," he said, snapping the book shut, "you're going to get that question right and it's going to be because of me and this watering can."

"Because of Mr. Leung, you mean."

"Because of the beans," said Mr. Leung, from the far row, without turning around.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Simple interest is calculated as I = P times r times t: the principal, times the annual interest rate, times the time in years.
story:
Alexis had forty minutes of lunch and a problem shaped like a number: two hundred dollars, which was what her uncle had offered to lend her for the secondhand camera she'd found online, except he'd said the words "five percent interest" in the same tone he used for weather forecasts, as if it were a fact of the atmosphere. She carried her tray to the table where Simona and Ernest were already arguing about whether the school's antiquated vending machines could legally sell anything that expired in 2019, and she set the tray down like evidence.

"I need someone who understands interest," she said.

Ernest raised a hand before swallowing. "I understand that I owe it. That's my area of expertise." He had a peccadillo for borrowing bus fare and repaying it in gum, which everyone had agreed years ago to find charming rather than irritating.

"That's the opposite of what I need," Alexis said, and pulled the camera listing up on her phone, turning the screen toward Simona. "My uncle will lend it. Five percent a year, he said, simple interest. But what does that actually cost me? Is five percent of everything I'll ever earn? Is it a trap? He said it like it was a courtesy."

Simona, who had a savings account because her grandmother opened one for her at nine, frowned at her yogurt. "Mine grows. The bank adds money every year because I leave it there. It's not much. But it goes up, not down." She wiggled her spoon as though demonstrating a physical law.

Alexis found a napkin and a pen that mostly worked. Two hundred dollars. Five percent a year. She wrote 200, then, underneath, the five percent as a decimal, 0.05, because Mr. Anderson had trained them all to convert before calculating, the way he made them convert before touching anything in the lab. Ten dollars a year, then. She checked it by multiplying 200 by 0.05 by 1, then by 2 for two years, and got twenty, and sat back.

"Twenty dollars," she said. "If I take two years to pay him back, the whole thing costs me twenty extra dollars."

"That's it?" Ernest said. "That's like two pizzas."

"It's principal times rate times time," Alexis said. "Two hundred, times point oh five, times two. Simple interest. He actually said it was simple. I thought he was being condescending."

Simona was doing something on her own napkin now, chewing the pen cap. "So if I put two hundred in my account and it's also five percent, and I leave it, then after two years..." She wrote, and her tongue went to the corner of her mouth. "Also twenty. But mine comes to me."

"That's a weird symmetry," Alexis said. "It costs me twenty to have the camera now, and it would cost Simona twenty to not have anything at all for two years." She looked at the napkin. The numbers were identical, facing opposite directions, which felt less like math and more like the kind of thing you could stand on either side of.

Fifth period, Mr. Anderson was demonstrating why certain metals ionize in water and others sulk at the bottom of the beaker, and Alexis, recording observations she'd copy properly later, kept drifting back to the napkin, which she'd folded into her pocket. She thought about how she'd spent the morning assuming her uncle was doing something to her, some financial gravity she couldn't see, when the whole time it was a number she could hold. That wasn't the same as knowing whether twenty dollars was a fair price for having the camera now instead of in the spring. That part didn't have a formula.

After last bell she found the pay phone by the gym, because her mother confiscated phones during exam week, a rule Alexis had once protested and now, dialing, found almost quaintly antiquated. Her uncle answered on the fourth ring.

"I'll take the loan," she said. "But I want to pay it back in one year, not two. Ten dollars is better than twenty."

There was a pause long enough that she could hear a television in the background. "You worked it out yourself?"

"Principal times rate times time," Alexis said. "I have a napkin to prove it."

"Keep the napkin," her uncle said, and she could hear him smiling, wherever he was, in front of whatever he was watching. "Frame it next to the camera."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Jesse arrived at the track with a binder under one arm and a bag of cones slung over his shoulder, and the first thing he saw was Jacob organizing the boys into a scrimmage, which was exactly the problem. For three weeks the under-fourteens had run games at every practice, full pitch, everyone shouting, and their passing had somehow gotten worse. Tonight he had a plan, and the plan had come from an unlikely place: a photocopy of a psychology study his sister left on the kitchen table, about violinists.

"You're late," Jacob said, tossing him the whistle.

"I'm exactly on time. You're early, which is suspicious." Jesse set down the cones. "No scrimmage tonight."

A groan went up from the boys, led by the sullen one, Danny, who had perfected the art of communicating disappointment through his shoulders alone. Jesse held up the binder. He had spent Sunday reading the study twice. In 1993, K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues had looked at violinists and found that the best ones did not simply log more hours; they did effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback. Scrimmage was hours. Scrimmage was what the whole team was already doing, cheerfully, endlessly, with no feedback except the scoreboard telling them they lost.

"Half of you can't complete a five-metre pass under pressure," Jesse said. "So we're going to fix that. Specifically. With drills that tell you immediately whether it worked."

"That sounds like homework," said Stefano, who was seventeen and helping out for community service hours and treated every sentence as an opening for negotiation.

"It's the opposite of homework. Homework is hours. This is effortful work on specific weaknesses. There's a whole study, violinists, 1993, Ericsson. They called it deliberate practice."

"Violinists," Danny said, with the contempt of a boy who had never voluntarily touched an instrument.

"Violinists, yes. They got better by fixing the exact thing they were bad at, not by playing whole songs over and over. Which is what a scrimmage is. A whole song. Badly." Jesse started laying cones in pairs, five metres apart. "So. Pairs. One ball. Pass through the gate, partner receives, passes back. Every miss, you both stop and say out loud what went wrong before you restart."

"That's embarrassing," said one of the smaller boys.

"That's feedback," Jesse said. "Immediate. It's the whole point."

They resisted, obviously. The first ten minutes were a sullen shuffle, balls rolling loose, Danny announcing "bad pass" in a monotone whenever his partner missed, which was technically compliance and spiritually sabotage. Jesse walked the line adjusting feet, saying "plant foot beside the ball, not behind it," and made each pair restart the moment a pass wobbled, and made them say what happened, every time. Slowly, the corrections got shorter. The gates got narrower. He started standing beside the receivers, tapping their shoulder a half-second before the pass arrived, and the smaller boys began to look up before receiving, which they had never once done in a scrimmage.

"You've operationalized nagging," Stefano observed, watching a pair complete twenty passes in a row while narrating their own errors like tiny commentators.

"It's science," Jesse said. "I operationalized the study."

Around minute forty, Jesse called a water break and crouched beside Danny, who was sulking on the ball bag. "You hate this."

"It's boring."

"You're also the best passer here."

Danny looked up, recalibrating.

"Which means," Jesse went on, "you get the hardest version. Tighter gates, and I'm going to stand in the passing lane and pressure you. Every time I block it, you tell me why." He stood and pulled a spare practice vest over his shirt. "Consider it a promotion."

They went twenty minutes more. When Jesse finally set up a small-sided game at the end, half pitch to keep the passing lanes short, Danny took the ball in traffic, looked up, and threaded a five-metre pass through two defenders to the smallest boy on the team, who scored, and the whole group erupted as though they'd won a cup. Even Jacob, who had guarded the scrimmage like an inheritance, was grinning.

"See," Jesse said, gathering cones as the light went orange over the far straightaway. "Next week, weaker foot."

"Week after that, can we just play?" Danny called from the gate, ball under his arm.

"Week after that," Jesse said, "we play better." He zipped the bag shut and jogged to catch up with them before the streetlights came on.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, launch angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range on level ground at the same speed.
story:
The launcher came in a box labeled physics department, surplus, and Ms. Mensah had signed it out to Brooke with one injunction: bring it back by Monday morning, intact, before first period. That gave them the weekend. The unit test was Monday afternoon, and Brooke had failed the last quiz so thoroughly that her mother had gone quiet at the kitchen table, which was worse than any lecture.

Saturday afternoon they set it up on the picnic table in Brooke's backyard: the launcher clamped to a board, a protractor taped to its hinge, a tape measure unspooleding across the grass toward the fence. Jackson brought a bag of the small yellow practice balls. Brennen came late, as always, carrying a slingshot he'd made in eighth grade and an insouciant grin that faded the moment he saw the launcher, which made the slingshot look like a toy.

"So you split it," Brooke said, reading from her notes. "The velocity. Horizontal and vertical components, and they don't talk to each other. Horizontal stays constant, vertical is just free fall." She had written it out four times Friday night, and each time it had dissolved on the page, the way a language she didn't speak dissolved when she tried to hold a sentence of it in her head. Her father had offered to help. He was an engineer, and his help had a way of becoming his success, so she had said no, and regretted it, and then not regretted it.

Jackson set the angle to thirty degrees. "Fire."

The ball arced out, dropped, bounced twice, and rolled to a stop. Brennen jogged a marker out and planted it in the grass where it had landed. They fired again at the same setting to be sure, and the second ball rolled to almost the same spot, close enough that they trusted the marker.

Then Jackson, who liked to break things before he understood them, cranked the launcher up to sixty degrees. "This one should go way farther," he said. "It's aimed at the sky instead of at the ground." Brooke had believed that too, an hour ago, which was part of what had made the quiz so bad. She had aimed all her answers low, treating the formulas like instructions for throwing a ball hard and flat, and every one had come back marked in red.

The ball went up in a high, lazy curve, seemed to hang, and came down. Brennen went to mark it and stopped. He stood over the grass for a second, then crouched. "It's basically on the flag."

They fired three more times at sixty, and twice at thirty, and the balls kept landing in the same small zone of grass, a scatter no wider than a bath towel. Jackson sat down on the picnic table itself, which he wasn't supposed to do. "That's broken," he said. "The launcher's broken."

Brooke looked at her notes. She had a formula for range on level ground and she worked through it twice on the back of the protractor's cardboard sleeve, with Brennen holding the sleeve steady against the wind. The sine of thirty and the sine of sixty sat there in her work like two halves of something. "They add to ninety," she said slowly. "Thirty and sixty. Complementary angles." The word surfaced from somewhere, a vocabulary sheet, a teacher's aside. "If the angles add up to ninety, same speed, flat ground, no air resistance, they land in the same place."

"You're making that up," Jackson said.

"I'm not making it up. It's in the math. Sixty goes high and comes down slow and short. Thirty goes flat and fast and runs out of room. Same spot." She said it with more certainty than she felt. The math said one thing and her instincts said another, and the grass said the math was right, but she couldn't have explained why the universe had arranged itself that way, and it bothered her that she couldn't. Brennen was already loading the launcher again, because Brennen trusted evidence over anyone's confidence, including his own.

They spent the next hour finding the edges of it. At forty-five the ball went clearly farther, past the marker zone, past the tape measure's end, and Brooke had to pace out the distance in sneaker lengths and convert it in her head. At ten degrees the balls fell so short they barely cleared the table's shadow, and at eighty they climbed like they meant to ionize into the blue overhead, then dropped nearly straight down into the same shallow band of range. Ms. Mensah would want the idealized version on Monday, the one without wind, without the drag that had made the sixty-degree balls drift a hand's width left each time. Brooke copied the practice problems into her notebook, then copied them again, and this time the sentences held their shape. She thought of her father, alone at the kitchen table with his coffee, and decided she would show him the notebook on Sunday, and let him ask her questions, and let herself not know some of the answers in front of him.

The sun was dropping behind the fence and the grass was going long-shadowed when Jackson checked his phone. "Two hours till I'm supposed to be home." Brennen set the launcher to fifteen degrees and looked at Brooke, waiting for the prediction before he fired. She looked down the tape measure, at the grass, at the angle, and held up her hand at a spot halfway to the marker.

"About there," she said. "Fire."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
Gavin's father had put the keys on the kitchen table the way other fathers apparently handed over a leather wallet and a speech about being a man. "Empty parking lot first," he said. "Then the ring road, if you don't kill us."

Gavin had a reason for wanting this license before September, and it wasn't the one he'd given. He'd told his father it was for the commute. Really it was that Leane had once said, at a party, laughing into her cup, that she'd never get in a car with a boy who couldn't drive, and Gavin had spent four months deciding whether that was a joke or a syllabus. Mannat, riding in the back seat with a bag of chips, knew the whole truth and had signed on as witness.

The parking lot went fine until it didn't. Gavin could park between two shopping carts with a centimetre to spare on either side, could reverse in a perfect arc, and had discovered that he liked the small mechanical certainties of the car, the way the wheel answered his hands. Then his father directed him onto the ring road, and something in Gavin changed. Every car ahead of him became an insult. He crept up on a hatchback until its bumper filled the windshield, then a van, then a hatchback again, adjusting without noticing that he was adjusting, closing the distance like the space itself was owed to him.

"Back off," his father said, mild, which was worse than shouting.

"I'm fine. He's going forty in a sixty."

"You're going forty too. Two metres behind him."

Mannat leaned between the seats. "My cousin failed for that twice. She'd creep up behind cars until the examiner just wrote it down. Her instructor finally fixed it with this thing, watch." He pointed through the windshield at an upcoming lamppost. "When the car ahead passes the lamppost, you count. One. Two. If you reach the lamppost before two seconds, you're too close. That's the two-second rule."

The hatchback slid past the lamppost. Gavin, transfixed by the bumper as if the gap between them could be closed by will alone, forgot to count. The lamppost arrived under the front wheels in what felt like half a heartbeat.

"Right," he said. "That."

They drove. Lampposts came every few seconds, sedimentary, layered along the road in even deposits, and Gavin counted out loud like a child learning a nursery rhyme. One. Two. One. Two. He was too close at every single one, which meant the problem had a shape now, a measurable wrongness, and shape was something he could work with. He eased off the accelerator until the counting landed. When he did it right, the road felt oddly slower and faster at once, the space ahead opening up like a held breath.

"You know," his father said, after a while, "I don't actually do that."

"Do what?"

"Count. I haven't counted at a lamppost in thirty years of driving." He looked out the side window. "I just know where the car should be. Or I think I do."

Gavin checked his mirror. There was a car close behind them, close the way he had been close, a driver who had been doing this for decades and had decided, somewhere along the way, that the gap was a suggestion. Mannat caught Gavin's eye in the mirror and raised an eyebrow. It occurred to Gavin that morning that there were two kinds of knowledge here, and that his father's kind had kept a family alive for thirty years, and that the counting kind had just saved Gavin from something he hadn't known he was doing. He could hold both. He wasn't sure yet whether experience was the distilled version of the rule or its revisionist enemy, whether time made you see the road better or just made you confident about seeing it worse. He only knew that for now, tonight, he was going to keep counting.

They pulled into the driveway at dusk. Gavin cut the engine and sat with his hands still on the wheel, and his father got out without a word, and Mannat collected his chip bag from the back seat. Through the windscreen Gavin watched Ms. Hamdan from next door watering her roses, unhurried, the hose moving in slow arcs.

"You're doing it again," Mannat said, following his gaze.

"I'm not doing anything."

"You're rehearsing a sentence about roses. I can hear it from here."

Gavin got out of the car and stood a moment in his own driveway, keys warm in his fist, still counting under his breath at nothing. Then he walked over to the fence.

"Ms. Hamdan," he said. "Do you ever need anything delivered?"

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
Caleb spread the two articles across the library table like cards he intended to play against each other. The first, from a glossy journal, reported that teenagers who kept handwritten journals reported lower stress; the study surveyed thirty students at a private school. The second, denser, gray with tables, reported the same finding from a survey of thirty thousand students across four countries. He had underlined the matching conclusions in both, in the same blue pen, and he wrote at the top of his notebook: both studies agree, therefore the finding is solid.

Benny dropped into the chair opposite him with a cafeteria cookie and no books. "You said you'd send me your chem notes by lunch."

"I'm doing the review for Papadopoulos."

"She'll take you three days early, she loves you. Notes. I'm failing without them." Benny slid the articles toward himself, squinting at the first page of each. "These both say the same thing. So write that. Two sources, same answer, done."

"It's not that simple."

"It is exactly that simple." Benny was already composing the text he would send if Caleb didn't, the message he'd drafted at midnight, half plea and half threat, and they both knew it. He wanted the notes the way a drowning man wants a rope, and he was not going to pretend otherwise.

Caleb pulled the articles back. "Tomorrow morning. Swear."

Benny left the cookie crumbs and went. Caleb read on, and the doubt arrived the way it does, sideways, through the small print. The small study listed a margin of error of plus or minus fourteen points. The large study listed one of one point. He sat with the two numbers for a long moment, then wrote, slowly: a bigger sample gives a more precise estimate. The same result from thirty people carries a much wider margin of error than the same result from thirty thousand. He looked at what he had written and felt the floor of his draft give way. Agreement was not the whole story. One of these findings was a guess; the other was nearly a measurement.

He took the notebook to the desk where Ms. Papadopoulos was cataloguing, because she had asked to see his articles when he'd chosen them. She turned the pages without hurry.

"Which one would you trust?" she said.

"The big one. The margin of error's tiny."

"There's your review, then."

"It's not that easy either. The big one surveyed all four countries together. The small one was one school. Maybe the small one is the only one actually about a school like mine." He heard himself and stopped, embarrassed by the sound of thinking out loud. She handed the pages back and said nothing, which he understood as permission.

He found a message from Ulysse waiting on his phone when he sat down again.

Hear me out. You always malign the small studies. That's your whole method. "Sample too small, throw it out." But the big survey lumped everyone together. Thirty people at one school tells you something thirty thousand averaged across a continent can't.

Caleb typed, deleted, typed again.

I'm not saying throw it out. I'm saying the same result with thirty people has a wider margin of error. With thirty thousand it's precise. That part's just true.

True and boring. Your review could just be the safe one. Mine's going to argue the small study matters more.

Mine's going to argue both, Caleb wrote, and hated how that sounded, and sent it anyway. Then he looked at the sentence until it stopped sounding like a dodge. Both, but not equally. He would weight the large study's precision against the small study's particularity, and he would say plainly, at the end, what he still could not decide: whether the small study's tight focus was worth its wide margin of error, or whether that margin swallowed its focus whole.

He started a fresh page. Across the room, the obsolescent card catalogue stood against the wall, drawers nobody opened anymore, and he thought, briefly and without knowing why, about how much of what he'd been certain of this morning was filed in a drawer like that. He wrote the first sentence of the review twice, crossed out the first version, and kept the second.

Benny texted at four: Notes???

Caleb photographed his chem notebook, all of it, and attached a line: You owe me a cookie. Then he went back to the draft, pen moving, the two articles side by side, the wide margin of error and the narrow one, neither one letting go of him yet.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The science museum had converted its side gallery into a temporary hall for the regional fair, and James's table sat between a display about bee cognition and a boy who had built a wind turbine from bicycle parts. In front of James stood three shallow dishes of copper sulfate crystals, blue as deep water, and beside them his lab notebook, open to a page where he had tried to transcribe his procedure so neatly that it looked like someone else's work. He was waiting for the judges, who were still two tables away, talking to the turbine boy in voices too low to hear.

Olivia came over first, coffee in hand, though the volunteers had told her twice that drinks weren't allowed in the gallery. "They weigh less," James said, before she could ask. "My crystals. I got out four point one grams, and I calculated I should have gotten six point nine." He turned the notebook toward her, where the arithmetic climbed the page in his cramped hand: the mass of his copper sulfate, divided by its molar mass, giving the moles of reactant; the moles carried across the balanced equation; the moles of product multiplied back up by a different molar mass into grams. "Six point nine grams theoretical. I did it three times."

"And you got four point one."

"Four point one actual."

Olivia picked up one of the dishes and tilted it so the crystals caught the light from the skylight. A woman in a museum uniform was moving along the far wall, straightening a banner about the planetarium's new show. Somewhere behind them, the turbine boy's blades ticked softly in a draft. "So is your math wrong," Olivia said, "or is your chemistry wrong?"

That was the question, and James had been circling it all morning without landing. He had done the mole calculation the way Mr. Chen had drilled them: mass in, molar mass, moles out, the stoichiometric bridge, molar mass again, mass out. He trusted it the way he trusted a staircase, each step holding weight. But he had also read, late at night, forums where people argued about filtration losses and water of crystallization, and those arguments ran on a different logic entirely, one of practical failure rather than clean proportion. He believed both things at once and did not yet know how to hold them together.

Mr. Chen arrived before the judges did. He had come on his day off, which James found quietly munificent of him, since Mr. Chen owed the fair nothing and had a long train ride home. He looked at the crystals, looked at the notebook, and slid his glasses up his nose. "Tell me what you told her," he said, so James told him: the mass, the molar mass, the moles, the six point nine grams he should have gotten. "Should have," Mr. Chen repeated, in a tone James couldn't read. "Or, calculated. What do you call it when you compare what you got to what you calculated?"

James looked at the page. The answer arrived not as a memory but as a recognition, the way a face resolves in a crowd. "Percent yield," he said. "The actual mass divided by the theoretical yield, times a hundred."

"Then do it."

James took the pen. Four point one divided by six point nine was roughly fifty-nine; times a hundred, fifty-nine percent. He wrote it down and the number sat on the page like a verdict, though he was honest enough with himself not to know what it was a verdict on. "Is that bad?" Olivia asked, and Mr. Chen only said, "It's his number," and stepped aside, because the judges had reached the bee table and would be at James's table in a minute.

The judge with the clipboard was younger than James expected, maybe a graduate student, and she asked him what he would do differently. He heard himself say that he didn't know yet whether the loss was in his handling or in the calculation's assumptions, that fifty-nine percent was a fact but not yet an explanation, and that he wanted to run it again both ways before he claimed to understand it. She wrote something down. Behind her, Olivia raised her coffee in a small toast, and the crystals stood in their dishes, holding the blue light, weighing exactly what they weighed.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Adolphe Thiers's History of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette and condemned radicals such as Robespierre.
story:
Clara spread her books across her grandmother's dining table, the one with the lace cloth folded back so as not to be ruined, and opened her laptop to a blank document titled only with the assignment's ugly abbreviation. The prompt wanted a historiographical essay, which Mr. Smith had described, in his dry way, as an essay not about the Revolution but about how people had written about the Revolution since 1800. She had been at the table for an hour and had produced one sentence, which she deleted because its second clause merely restated its first, and even she could see that it was tautological, a sentence chasing its own tail.

The problem wasn't the reading. She had the reading spread around her like fallen leaves. The problem was that every historian she read seemed to be arguing with someone who wasn't in the room. A conservative writing in the 1850s raged at men dead for decades. A Marxist writing in the 1920s treated those same men as instruments of forces they could not have named. She could summarize each one, but the assignment asked for something she couldn't yet locate: her own considered position among them, stated honestly, including what she could not decide.

Her grandmother's house smelled of cardamom and old paper, and on the third afternoon Clara wandered into the study while the kettle heated. The shelves held her grandfather's books, untouched since his death two springs ago. She ran a finger along the spines and stopped at a set of crumbling volumes in French, their leather gone soft as fruit. She recognized the name on the spines because she had seen it that morning in her reading, in a footnote she had skipped past. Thiers.

She carried the first volume to the table and opened it, and the flashback arrived before she asked it to. She was eleven, in this same study, and her grandfather was showing her a book about prehistoric horses, tracing with his pencil how the little forest animal changed over epochs into something that could run on open plains. He had used the word phylogeny, the history of how a lineage changes through time, and she had repeated it until it lost its shape in her mouth. He said ideas had lineages too. She had thought he was being poetic. Now she sat with a French history written by a Frenchman about events his own parents might have witnessed, and she wondered whether histories had phylogenies, whether each generation's account descended with variations from the last.

She texted Yan, who was doing the same assignment and complaining about it in a group chat with Ayva. Clara typed: I found something. Come over.

They arrived within the hour, Ayva with her shoes already untied in anticipation of taking them off. Clara laid the volume open and showed them the publication dates in the front matter, 1823 through 1827, and the pages she had worked through with her grandmother's dictionary at her elbow. "He praises Mirabeau and Lafayette," she said, "the moderates, the ones who tried to slow it down. And he goes after Robespierre. Hard."

Yan frowned at the French. "Who cares? He's some old writer."

"That's what I thought. Then I looked him up." She turned her laptop so they could see the encyclopedia entry. Thiers had not just written about the Revolution. Decades later he had run France, as its head of government, putting down the Paris Commune in the streets. Ayva read it twice, and Yan said, slowly, "So he wrote the history before he made some."

The sentence sat among the three of them like something set down carefully on the lace cloth. Clara felt the tiredness that had begun to enervate her all week drain away into something sharper. Here was a man who had judged the Revolution's radicals from a desk, then faced actual radicals himself and shot them. His book was not a lie, she thought, or not only a lie. It was a position, held by a person standing somewhere specific, and once you saw where he stood, the shape of his praise became legible. Not discredited. Legible.

They worked until the light went amber. Ayva argued that this meant all the histories were just politics wearing costume, and Yan pushed back that Mathiez, the one she was reading, had dug up archives nobody had touched and corrected real errors, which was not nothing. Clara wrote nothing down for a long time. Then she opened her document and typed a paragraph that began with Thiers and the dates, 1823 to 1827, and ended with a sentence she was almost embarrassed by its plainness: that accounts of the Revolution seemed to change less because new facts emerged than because the writers kept standing in new places, and that she could not yet say whether this made the histories worthless or simply made them evidence of a second kind.

She read it aloud to them. Ayva said she thought it was arguable, which from Ayva was praise. Yan pulled one of the crumbling volumes toward her and squinted at a margin note in her grandfather's small, upright hand. "There's writing in here," Yan said. "Look."

Clara leaned over her friend's shoulder, and read the faded pencil line her grandfather had left beside Thiers's condemnation of Robespierre, forty years before she was born: "Check who benefits."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
The laminated menu in Levi's hand said GIOVANNI'S FAMILY TABLE in a font that belonged on a pasta jar, and beneath it, in smaller print, NOW HIRING. He had walked past the restaurant four times that week, and on the fifth time the manager, a broad man with a towel over one shoulder, noticed him hesitating and said, "You want a job or you want to stare at the calamari?" Levi said the first thing that came to him, which was "Both, ideally," and somehow that got him an interview on Saturday.

He told Brenna about it at school, holding his phone up like evidence. "Bussing tables. Weekend shifts. Minimum wage, which is still money, which is still a car eventually." Brenna peered at the screen. "You, with a career in dirty dishes. My grandmother would say you're learning humility. I say you're learning where the good tips are." Andreanne, who had worked at a frozen yogurt place all last summer, told him the only rule that mattered: never trust the schedule until you've photographed it.
