"Schedules are living documents," she said solemnly, as though reciting scripture. "They mutate."

The first two weeks were mostly carrying tubs and apologizing to a waiter named after a saint. Then winter break arrived and the holiday rush with it, and the manager began asking, every other night, whether Levi could stay later, come in earlier, cover for someone's cousin's wedding. Levi kept saying yes, partly for the money and partly because saying no to the manager felt like contradicting a small and weary despot whose kingdom was a floor of checked tile. He photographed every schedule anyway, per Andreanne's commandment.

At the end of the second week of break, he opened his pay stub in the parking lot and stood very still beside the dumpster. Some of his hours had been paid at a higher rate than the others. He read the numbers twice, then three times, as if the ink might rearrange itself. His first thought was that the payroll system had made an error in his favor, a concept so foreign to his experience of institutions that he nearly went back inside to report it, which, Brenna later pointed out, would have made him the most honest sixteen-year-old in the county and also a fool.

Instead he ruminate over it that night, spread out with the stub and his photographed schedules on the kitchen table, counting hours on his fingers like a much younger person. Fifty-two hours in the week. Anything past forty, he remembered dimly, from somewhere in a semester of a class he'd half-slept through, had to be paid more. He texted Andreanne: is there a thing where hours over 40 are paid at like one and a half times your normal rate. She replied within a minute, in the tone of someone quoting her old supervisor: "Overtime. One and a half times your regular rate, for hours past forty in a workweek." Then: "you worked 52 hours?? you absolute machine."

So the payroll system had not erred. It had simply known the law better than he did, which stung a little, though not as much as the discovery of what he still didn't know: whether the manager had scheduled him past forty on purpose, or had simply been swimming in the same ignorance Levi had. He turned the question over for a day. It mattered, he decided, because the difference between someone who didn't know and someone who did but hoped you wouldn't was the difference between a tired man and a cheat, and he wanted to believe the tired man, and he also wanted his money either way.

On Monday he found the manager stacking chairs before opening. "I worked fifty-two hours last week," Levi said, and then, because the sentence needed an ending, "and I noticed the extra rate on the hours past forty." The manager set down a chair, looked at him for a long moment, and scratched his jaw. "You counted your own hours." "I photographed my schedule and then I counted." The manager made a sound that was almost a laugh. "My accountant handles that," he said. "I just put names in boxes." Levi couldn't tell if that was an excuse or a confession, and suspected it might be both, or neither.

He rode home in the cold with the pay stub folded in his jacket pocket, and the atavistic satisfaction of having hunted down an answer still humming in him, some old part of his brain convinced it had tracked a large animal through snow. He texted Brenna a picture of the stub with no caption. She replied with three applause emojis and then, in a separate message, "next: teach me." "Come to the restaurant," Levi typed back. "Tuesday. I'll get you the good table."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Canada's Rand formula, from Justice Ivan Rand's 1946 ruling after a Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario, requires all workers covered by a union contract to pay dues.
story:
Connor had been at the warehouse for six weeks when he noticed the second deduction. He stood at the break room table with his pay stub flattened under one palm, reading it the way you read a credit card statement, line by line, looking for the thing that shouldn't be there. Nine dollars and change, labelled only "dues." He had never joined anything.

"That's the union," said Francesca, sliding her mug into the microwave. She worked the station next to his, the one where the scanner beeped twice for every box because the trigger stuck. "Everybody pays it."

"But I didn't sign up." He turned the stub over as though the back might apologize. "Nobody asked me."

She shrugged and waited for the microwave to finish its hum. "Take it up with Hallie. She's the steward's kid." Hallie was their shift lead, twenty, loud about everything except the things she was actually loud about. When she came through at eleven with the replenishment sheets, Connor caught her by the rack of empty pallets and showed her the stub.

"Never joined," he said. "I looked. There's no form with my name on it."

Hallie glanced at the number, then at him, deciding something. "You don't have to join. It's the law, out of a ruling. Justice Ivan Rand, 1946, after the Ford strike in Windsor, Ontario. Every worker covered by a union contract pays dues, member or not." She handed the stub back. "They call it the Rand formula."

"That's it? No choice?"

"You got a shift premium this month, right?" She tapped the top of the stub, where an extra line added forty dollars he hadn't earned. "Somebody fought for that in the seventies. You weren't born. You still cash the cheque." She walked off with her sheets, and he stood there holding his whole argument, which had suddenly gotten lighter.

The trouble was that his father, who had driven him to the interview and waited in the parking lot with the radio on, called unions "a profligate tax on a kid's first paycheque" that same night, over dinner. His father had never been in one. He had also never had a shift premium, Connor realized, or maybe he had and had never thought about who had asked for it. Both of them, father and son, tended to valorize the self-made worker, the man who owes nobody, and Connor was starting to suspect that this picture left out a lot of the frame. He didn't say any of this at the table. He said, "Pass the ketchup," and thought about it on the drive to work the next morning.

That week the manager announced that the Friday shift would run two hours longer, unpaid past the second one due to a "rounding practice" nobody had heard of before. Hallie filed a grievance by Thursday. On Friday at shift end, Connor watched the manager and Hallie standing by the time clocks, her with a binder, him with his arms crossed, and then, at 10:58, the manager waving everyone out with the back of his hand like a man shooing birds. Hallie caught Connor's eye across the floor and pointed at the clock with her chin.

"So it works," Connor said later, in the parking lot, engine running, Francesca leaning in his passenger window because her ride was late.

"It works sometimes." She spat a sunflower seed shell into the dark. "It also costs you nine bucks a cheque for the rest of your life. My mom says think of it like insurance. My dad says think of it like an externality, the cost of something you didn't choose landing on you anyway." She frowned at her own sentence. "Except I think he's using it wrong. He does that."

He drove home with both windows down, working it through. His father's version was simple: money out, nothing back, theft. The parking lot version was also simple: dues in, grievance out, fair trade. The truth he could actually defend was less tidy. The Rand formula meant he paid for a contract he never signed, and that same contract had just handed him two hours of his life back on a Friday night. Whether the nine dollars a cheque was a fair price for that, he couldn't say yet, and he noticed he didn't much want to say it, because either answer made him look like somebody's son.

On Monday his stub was waiting in the envelope by the time clocks, and there was the deduction again, same amount, no explanation, and beside it the premium, and beside that the corrected hours from Friday, which the payroll clerk had written in green ink with a small check mark, like a grade.

Connor folded the stub in half and put it in his shirt pocket, then took it out and looked at it once more under the clock light.

"Still not a member," he said to Hallie, passing her on his way in.

"Still paying," she said, and tossed him a scanner with the sticky trigger.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: If a Java class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one; once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added.
story:
The deadline was midnight, and Jordan had until then to submit a class called Book with private fields, getter methods, and a test that proved they worked. His grandmother's kitchen smelled of onions and old newspaper, and the wireless router lived on top of the grandfather clock, which meant the signal was strongest if he sat with his laptop on the hallway floor with his back against the radiator. He sat with his laptop on the hallway floor with his back against the radiator.

He had written the class two days earlier, in the before-times, when it was simple: private String title, private double price, a getTitle method, a getPrice method, no constructor at all. The test had passed. Then Alden had texted him a suggestion, which was Alden's way of issuing homework: you should add a constructor that takes the title and price, it looks more professional. Jordan had added it. He was a canny enough student to keep the old test file rather than delete it, which was the only reason he still had evidence of what had worked before.

Now the old test failed on its first line. Book b = new Book, the parentheses empty, and underneath it a red squiggle like something had died there.

He messaged Alden. "Did your old tests break too?"

"Mine never passed to begin with," Alden wrote back. "Different problem. Beautiful in its way."

Jordan's grandfather came down the hall with a mug of tea and stood over him the way he stood over the crossword, not helping, just weather. "You look like a man exhuming something," he said.

"A test. It worked on Monday. I only added one thing since then." Jordan scrolled between the two files. The class had a constructor now, a real one with a title and a price in its parentheses. The old test still asked for a Book with nothing in the parentheses at all, as if that were still a thing you could ask for.

"The dead rise," his grandfather said, and went back to the kitchen.

Nathanael called at nine, because Nathanael never texted when he could call. "Ms. Santoso extended the deadline once already, she's not doing it twice," he said. "I heard her tell the other section that midnight means midnight. What's your problem, exactly?"

"I had a test. It passed. Then I wrote a constructor that takes parameters, and now the old test says it can't make a Book with no arguments, like the empty-parentheses version stopped existing."

There was a pause on the line, the sound of Nathanael thinking with his mouth open. "Oh," he said. "Oh, that's the thing she mentioned in the notes nobody read. If you don't write any constructor, the compiler adds a default one for you, with no arguments. But once you write any constructor, the default one isn't added anymore. So your old test is asking for something that isn't there."

Jordan looked at the screen. It was strange, the way the fact sat there, unglamorous and total: the empty-parentheses Book had never been something he'd built. It had been something given, quietly, and he had spent two days not knowing it was a gift. "So Monday's version worked because of something I didn't write."

"Everything's like that," Nathanael said. "Cities work like that. You don't notice the bridge until it falls down." Nathanael was applying to colleges to study economics, and he called things like bridges and default constructors "externalities," which Jordan had looked up once and still half-mistrusted. The word seemed to let people charge you for things you never agreed to, or forgive you for things you never noticed. Both, maybe.

There were two roads and time for one. He could write a second constructor, an empty one with nothing in its parentheses, so the old test's request existed again. Or he could change the old test, make it pass a title and a price like the new constructor wanted, and keep only the version he had chosen. The first way kept everything; the second way admitted that something had been lost.

He wrote the empty constructor. He ran the old test, and it passed, and then he ran the new one, and that passed too, and the green checkmarks stacked up in the console like tiles. Both tests green, everything working, and yet he felt obscurely like he had paid for it, that the empty constructor was a small monument to a version of his code that no longer existed on its own terms. He submitted at 11:42.

His grandfather passed through the hall again on his way up to bed. "Solved?"

"Solved. Mostly." Jordan closed the laptop halfway, like a mouth about to speak.

"Mostly is the honest answer to everything," his grandfather said, and paused on the stairs with his hand on the rail. "Come look at the clock before you sleep. It's been running slow all week and I can't decide whether to fix it or let it drift."

Jordan followed him up the stairs.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
story:
The trouble began with the box in the back of Koen's car, which had sat in the sun through a whole afternoon of lacrosse practice. When Cohen lifted the lid, the chocolates inside looked ruined, streaked with a dull grey film, whitish and blotchy, like frost on a window that had been breathed on and left. He had spent his last paycheque from the garden centre on that couverture, and the bake sale that was supposed to rescue the robotics club's travel fund was tomorrow at ten.

"They still smell fine," Hope said, leaning over his shoulder in Koen's kitchen. She was the one who had volunteered the venue, partly because her kitchen had a marble countertop and partly because her mother worked nights and would not be there to ask questions.

"Smell isn't the problem." Cohen broke a piece off and it bent instead of snapping, then crumbled greasily between his fingers. He had been reading about chocolate for two weeks, mostly at one in the morning, and somewhere in the forums he had seen a photograph of chocolate that looked exactly like this. The word floated back to him. "Fat bloom."

"What's that?"

"That streaky grey stuff. It happens when chocolate isn't tempered right, or when it melts and resets." He turned the piece over in the light. "It's still chocolate. It just looks like something you'd find in a shed."

Koen came in with his gym bag and peered at the box with the pitying expression of a pundit delivering a verdict. "Nobody buys chocolate that looks like that," he said. "They'll walk past our table and buy Hope's lemon squares."

"Then we melt it down and start over," Cohen said. "That's the whole thing about tempering. You melt it, you cool it while you work it, and if you do it right it sets shiny and it snaps." He had never actually done it. The forums were full of people who had never actually done it, which was part of why he trusted none of them completely.

The recipe of the evening went like this: chop the chocolate, reserve a third, melt the rest in a bowl over simmering water without letting any steam condense into it, then seed the bowl with the reserved chunks and stir until they dissolved, dragging the temperature down. Mr. Somsak, the neighbour from across the fence, had come over to complain about the noise of the extractor fan and stayed to watch, arms folded, offering nothing except the observation that his own mother had tempered chocolate in Bangkok using a marble slab and a spatula and no thermometer at all. Cohen found this both comforting and useless. He trusted the thermometer. He also understood, standing there stirring in slow figure eights while Hope read the numbers aloud, that the thermometer could only tell him where he was, not whether he would get where he wanted to go.

The first batch went wrong. He had been impatient, had seeded too much at once, and the chocolate thickened around the unmelted chunks like something swallowing them. He stood over the bowl with his hands on the edge of the counter, feeling the peculiar impecuniousness of a boy who could not afford to waste another two hundred grams. It was Koen, surprisingly, who spoke first. "It's like the cooling loop on the printer," he said. "You don't dump the whole cold reservoir in. You bleed it in." Cohen looked at him, then back at the bowl, and felt two ways of thinking about a problem settle against each other and click, the way he imagined gears must. Not that he would have said that out loud.

They remelted and tried again, bleeding the seed in a spoonful at a time while Hope called the temperature like a coxswain. At thirty-one degrees the chocolate ran off the spatula in a smooth ribbon that hardened on the marble within a minute, and Cohen, hardly breathing, touched the corner of a test smear. It was glossy. He broke it and it snapped, a clean bright crack, and Mr. Somsak said "ah" in a tone that made up for the extractor fan.

At eleven that night they had seventy pieces setting in rows, dark and gleaming, and the bloomed originals chopped and sealed for next time, because Cohen intended there to be a next time. "So we're done?" Koen said, already reaching for his phone.

"We're done if it's still shiny at nine in the morning," Cohen said. He carried the tray to the coolest corner of the pantry, set it down flat, and closed the door halfway, leaving it open exactly the width of his hand.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
Seth spread the newspapers across the kitchen table like a geologist confronting a particularly stubborn sedimentary deposit, three weeks of mail his mother had meant to sort and had not, with the Arabic papers his neighbor saved for him pressed somewhere near the bottom. Ms. Kobayashi, who took two dailies and never finished either, had said, "You want them, take them, they sediment," which was not quite the word but had stuck in the house anyway. On top of the pile, his phone lay face up, Delphine's face filling the screen.

"You promised," she said. "Eight o'clock, you summarize one article live, on camera, and if you don't freeze, I put you on the world news segment Thursday. I need a second voice, Seth. If it's just me talking for ten minutes, the club will vote to cancel us, and then it's back to the bake sale, and I refuse to be the girl whose legacy is brownies."

"You'll be fine," Seth said. "Your legacy is very brownie-resistant."

"Read the article."

He unfolded the Cairo paper and found a short piece, four paragraphs, about a shipping dispute in the Gulf. He read the first sentence aloud and immediately felt the ground shift under him. He knew Arabic, or he had always believed he knew Arabic, the Arabic of his grandmother's kitchen, of her instructions about onions and her teasing about his posture. This was the same alphabet and it was not the same language. The words sat on the page like relatives he recognized at a funeral but could not name.

"That's not what you spoke at your grandma's," Delphine said, unhelpfully, from the counter where the phone was propped against the sugar jar.

"Thank you, yes, I noticed."

He tried again, sounding it out, and the sentence came out flat and wrong, like a song played at the wrong speed. His grandmother's Arabic would have said it differently, he was almost sure, softer in some places, chopped in others. He got through the second paragraph, understood perhaps two words in five, and put the paper down. He texted her, then remembered she answered texts on Tuesdays, by which she meant she looked at her phone on Tuesdays, and it was Friday.

He tried the other paper instead, the one Ms. Kobayashi got from the Lebanese grocer, and found a story on the same shipping dispute. Different paper, different country, four hundred miles of coastline between them. And the sentences moved the same way. Same stiff, formal rhythm, same words he half-knew. He read a line from the Cairo piece, then a line from the Beirut piece, back and forth, and it was like two people from two different cities reading from the same hymnbook. He sat with that for a minute, the way you sit with a puzzle piece that turns out to fit two places at once.

"Delphine," he said slowly, "you know how my grandma talks, and how her cousin from the village talks, and they argue about whose Arabic is the correct one, forever, at every wedding?"

"Fondly."

"The newspapers aren't doing that. Both papers, both countries, and it's one kind of Arabic on the page. The one that isn't the way anybody I know talks." He flipped between them again to be sure. "It's called Modern Standard Arabic. It's in the little label on the masthead page, I just found it." He laughed, short and surprised. "So there's a version of the language just for writing, and it's the same for readers in all these different places, and nobody's grandmother argues about it because nobody's grandmother speaks it at anybody."

Delphine made a noise that in club terms counted as applause. "Great. Now do it on camera. Summarize the article, out loud, sixty seconds, no notes on the facts, notes on the words are allowed because I'm merciful."

He set the phone against the sugar jar where her face had been and cleared his throat. He rebuilt the article in his head, the chronology of it, the tanker detained, the clause that promised to indemnify the shipping company if the cargo was seized, the company saying the clause did not apply. He began, haltingly, in the newspaper's own language, the formal one that belonged to everyone and no one's kitchen, and somewhere in the second sentence he heard his grandmother's rhythm slip in underneath it, and he let it stay.

"That was forty seconds," Delphine said, "and you only made up one word. Thursday. You're on Thursday. Wear the blue shirt."

"Which blue shirt?"

"You have one blue shirt, Seth. Your grandma told me."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: The term 'unreliable narrator' was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
story:
Julia spread the novel open on the kitchen table and pressed it flat with two hands, as if it might bolt. The essay was due first period, and she had four paragraphs that said nothing she believed. Maram sat across from her with a mug of tea gone cold, reading Julia's draft upside down, which she claimed helped her see the structure. Outside, the neighbour's sprinkler ticked across the lawn in its slow arcs, and the long grass undulated in the evening wind like something breathing.

"You wrote that the narrator lies," Maram said. "Twice. Both times."

"He does lie." Julia turned the pages of the novel to the passage she'd marked, the one where the narrator insists he was kind to his brother, though every other detail in the chapter proved the opposite. The strange thing was that she believed him anyway, every time, for about a page, before the evidence caught up with her. That was what she wanted to write about, and she couldn't get it into sentences.

"Mr. Bennett wrote that on my last essay," she said. "You used the term without saying where it comes from. Just a note in the margin. I figured it was, like, a thing everyone knows." She had put unreliable narrator in her first sentence tomorrow's draft and felt proud of it for exactly one evening, until she'd realized she couldn't answer the simplest question about it. Where had she learned it? Nowhere, really. It had drifted into her vocabulary the way words do, through reviews and class discussions and half-remembered videos, and she'd been using a phrase she couldn't source.

The deadline sat on the whiteboard by the fridge in her mother's handwriting: essay due tomorrow, orthodontist Thursday. Julia got up and paced the length of the kitchen, which took four steps. "It's a term, though. Somebody made it up. Somebody had to be first."

"Google it," Maram said, in the tone of someone offering an obvious kindness.

She did, and the screen gave her more than she wanted at first, article after article, until she narrowed it down. The critic Wayne C. Booth had coined the term, in 1961, in a book called The Rhetoric of Fiction. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, because something about it rearranged her whole essay in her head. The phrase she'd been using like air was only sixty-some years old. Before Booth, readers had still suspected their narrators, surely, but there'd been no handle for the suspicion, no name to hang it on. She said it out loud to test it. "Wayne C. Booth, 1961, The Rhetoric of Fiction. He coined the term."

"Put that in the essay," Maram said.

"I'm putting it in the essay."

But the fact alone wasn't the argument, and she knew it. She sat back down and started a new page in her notebook, because the laptop screen made her draft look finished when it wasn't. At the top she wrote: two ways to read him. Under the first she wrote that the narrator was a liar, full stop, and the book was a puzzle where you dug for the truth underneath. Under the second she wrote that the lying was the point, that the voice was the experience, and the reader's doubled trust and distrust was a kind of symbiosis, the narrator needing her belief even while he destroyed it. She looked at the word and decided she meant it. The book couldn't work without her, and she couldn't get the story without him.

The problem was that both readings were true and they pulled against each other. Her father came through the kitchen on his way to the garage and paused at the table long enough to say it looked like a séance, four books open, the kettle on, Maram mouthing sentences along with Julia as she read them. Julia waved him off without looking up. The clock over the stove said nine. The essay needed to be printed by eleven, because the printer was capricious and her mother had decreed no morning printing, not after the incident in March.

She typed the Booth sentence into her second paragraph and then sat with her hands off the keys, staring at it. The fact anchored her, but it also opened something she hadn't expected. If a critic had to invent the term, then distrust of a narrator wasn't natural, it was a way of reading that someone had to build, and she was learning to build it too, tonight, at this table. And there was a question she couldn't close down: whether Booth's name for the thing had changed the thing itself, whether readers after 1961 read differently because they had a word for their suspicion. She wrote that question into the last paragraph and then, instead of answering it, wrote that she didn't know, and that the not knowing seemed honest, and that her own trust in the narrator kept shifting depending on which chapter she'd last read.

Maram read the final draft right side up this time, slowly, with her cold tea between her palms. "It's better," she said. "It sounds like you arguing with yourself."

"It's me losing," Julia said, but she was already pulling the laptop toward the printer cable, winding it tight, coaxing the connection. The printer groaned, considered, and pushed out the first page while Julia held the tray steady with one hand, watching each line appear.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly 3 million volts per metre, which limits how strong a field can be across an air gap.
story:
The physics exhibit occupied the museum's east wing, a long crepuscular hall where the overhead lights had been dimmed to make the glowing displays feel like constellations. Camille stood at the plate capacitor station with her worksheet clipped to a clipboard, trying to compute the electric field strength at the midpoint between two charged plates. The formula was simple enough on paper, field strength equals voltage divided by separation, but the numbers kept refusing to behave.

"Did you get yours?" Kaitlin asked, leaning over from the next station, where a plasma ball fizzled purple under her palm.

"Almost. The plates here run at four thousand volts, and the gap is one millimetre." Camille wrote the division out twice, checking herself, and the answer arrived the same way both times: four million volts per metre. She circled it, then uncircled it, because the number had a look she distrusted, the look of something too large to have been hiding in a museum exhibit.

Tiago appeared behind them with his phone out, comparing answers with two boys from the other section. "What did you two get for the field?" he asked. Camille turned her clipboard face down on the railing before she answered, and said, casually, that she was still checking her units. That was technically true. She wanted to be sure first, alone, that the arithmetic was hers and not borrowed.

Ms. Morningstar, their physics teacher, was across the hall at the Van de Graaff generator, arranging the students into a line for the hair-raising demonstration. She had told them on the bus that the museum trip would count as a lab, that the worksheet was due before they left, and that she would answer no questions about it. "The exhibits are the teacher today," she had said, in the flat voice she used for rules.

Camille redid the calculation a third time. Four thousand volts across one millimetre was four thousand volts across one thousandth of a metre, which was four million volts per metre. There was no confounder she could find, no place where a stray factor of ten had crept in. She was about to write the answer in ink when Tiago, still hovering, caught the edge of her reasoning even with the clipboard flipped.

"Wait, what voltage did you say those plates run at?"

"Four thousand. Why?"

He held up his own worksheet, where he had sketched the same plates with a different number written beside them, a number she could not read at that angle. He was smiling in the particular way he smiled when he had caught something. "Because I think your air is about to betray you," he said. "Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly three million volts per metre. That limits how strong a field can be across an air gap."

Camille looked at the exhibit, then at her clipboard, then at the exhibit again. The plates sat there, dull and inert behind their acrylic case, separated by a gap she could have covered with a fingernail. If her number was right, the field between them exceeded what air could hold. Either the museum had built an exhibit that spat lightning at schoolchildren, or she had made an error she could not yet see, or the plates were not doing what the placard implied.

"Read the placard again," Kaitlin said. Camille did. The placard specified four hundred volts, not four thousand; the tens place had been worn nearly smooth by years of visitors rubbing it with their thumbs, and in the dim light she had read a zero that was not there. Her stomach dropped, then settled. She recalculated slowly, deliberately, making herself wait through each step: four hundred volts across a thousandth of a metre, four hundred thousand volts per metre, comfortably below the limit Tiago had named. Below it by more than a factor of seven. The air between the plates could subsume that field without complaint, could hold it the way glass holds light, and nothing would spark.

She wrote the answer in ink. Then she sat with it for a moment, because the correction did not dissolve her unease so much as reshape it. The formula had not changed, and neither had the plates, and yet the meaning of her arithmetic had depended entirely on a digit half-erased by strangers' fingers. She believed her new answer, but she noticed that she believed it in a different way than she had believed the old one: provisionally, with the placard's worn surface still in her mind.

Across the hall, Ms. Morningstar clapped twice and called the class to gather for the demonstration. Tiago offered Camille a fist to bump, and she bumped it, but she did not put the clipboard away. She stood at the railing a few seconds longer, looking at the gap between the plates, the thin bright corridor of air where nothing was happening and, as far as she could now tell, nothing would.

"Camille," Kaitlin called from the doorway. "It's starting."

She looked up. "Coming," she said, and clicked her pen closed.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The three primary chords of a major key are built on its first, fourth and fifth notes, so in C major they are C, F and G.
story:
The studio smelled of dust and rosin, the way it had every Tuesday since September, and Liam set his notebook on the music stand before he took off his coat. Sixteen blank bars of staff paper, drawn with a ruler the night before, waited under the small brass lamp. Ms. Yamamoto was tuning the piano in the corner, striking A above middle C and leaning toward the string as though listening for a lie.

"You've brought something," she said, without turning around.

"Half of something." He opened the notebook to the melody he'd written, eleven bars that wandered up when he wanted them to settle. In the margins Mason had scrawled encouragement two nights ago, sprawled on Liam's bedroom floor with his guitar across his chest, playing the same three chord shapes over and over. Mason could only play three chords, and he played them with total conviction, like a man who owned exactly three doors and used all of them daily.

"Play it for me," Ms. Yamamoto said, so Liam did, picking out the line one finger at a time. It fell apart at bar nine. He knew it fell apart; he'd known it for three days, and the knowing had sat in him like a stone in a shoe.

"Here's my problem," he said. "Mason keeps telling me to just pick three chords and build everything on them. And I keep thinking that's lazy. Like it's cheating to use so little." He heard how grandiose that sounded as soon as he'd said it, a seventeen-year-old defending the integrity of sixteen bars against a friend with a secondhand guitar, and he felt his ears go warm.

Ms. Yamamoto sat down on the piano bench and folded her hands. "Which three does he play?"

"C, F, and G. He says every song he likes uses them. I figured he was exaggerating."

She didn't answer that. Instead she said, "Show me a C chord," and watched while he found it, white keys only, sounding hollow and certain at once. "Now start on the first note of the scale and count up. One, C. Which note is four?"

Liam counted under his breath. "F." He played an F chord and it opened under his fingers like a room he hadn't known was in the house.

"And five?"

"G." The G chord had a tilt to it, a kind of leaning. He sat with all three for a moment, playing them in the order Mason always played them, C to F to G, and something in the melody's ninth bar stopped feeling like a failure and started feeling like a question the chords could answer. "So the three primary chords of a major key," he said slowly, "are built on the first, fourth, and fifth notes. In C major that's C, F, and G. That's the whole reason his three chords work. It's not that he's lazy. He found the load-bearing walls."

"Did he find them, or did he trip over them?"

"That's the part I can't tell," Liam admitted. "Whether knowing why makes the thing better or just makes it harder to play." He had been trying all week to dichotomize his music into two piles, the felt and the understood, and the piles kept leaking into each other. Mason didn't know a fourth from a fifth and his playing still made people lean in. Liam could name every interval on the page and his melody had died at bar nine anyway.

Ms. Yamamoto laughed, a short, low sound. "I studied epidemiology before I studied music," she said, rising to sharpen a pencil at the desk by the window. "I spent two years tracking how things spread through populations. Chords are not so different. They move through songs, through decades, through whole cities of teenagers with guitars. You can map the spread or you can catch the thing. Mason caught it."

Liam pulled the notebook closer and wrote F under bar nine, then G under bar thirteen, and began filling the sixteenth bar with a long C, held across the whole measure. Some questions he would keep, the way you keep a stone in your pocket to know it's there: whether understanding would ever feel as clean as Mason's ignorance, whether the melody would be his or just the chords wearing his tune. He put his hands on the keys.

"From the top," he said.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm monitors and the noxious floor cleaner the janitor had dragged through at lunch, and Kaylee sat in the third row with her query returning seventeen rows when it should have returned six. Ms. Chan had set the problem on the board in plain words: find the customers who had never ordered anything. Two tables, Customers and Orders, joined in a way that kept the ones with no match. That was all. It had taken Kaylee forty minutes to understand that the forty minutes had been spent understanding nothing.

"It's pronounced sequel," Trevor said two seats over, not looking up from his screen. "Everybody says sequel."

"Everybody is wrong," Karlee said. She had her boots on the rung of her chair and her arms crossed, which was how she argued, all posture. "It's S-Q-L. Three letters. You spell out acronyms."

Kaylee typed SELECT and then stopped, her fingers resting on the keys. She had been saying sequel in her head all semester, the way you absorb the weather without deciding to. Now she turned in her chair. "Why would people say sequel if it's spelled SQL?"

Trevor swiveled around, delighted to have a third party. "Because it used to be spelled that way. My cousin works at IBM, he said it was developed there in the early seventies by these two guys, Chamberlin and Boyce, and it was first called SEQUEL. So the pronunciation is the fossil. The letters changed and the sound stayed."

"Your cousin also said you could get into State," Karlee said, but Kaylee was already typing it into the search bar, because that was the kind of thing Trevor half remembered, and half remembered things were either true or invented, and you couldn't tell from the telling. The pages loaded. Chamberlin and Boyce, IBM, early 1970s, first called SEQUEL. All of it, exactly as he'd said, which was somehow worse than if he'd made it up, because now she owed him being right.

"So it's sequel," Kaylee said.

"It's sequel," Trevor agreed, and Karlee made a low sound of contempt and turned back to her screen, and the argument ended the way their arguments always ended, with nothing settled and everyone satisfied.

But the word stayed with her while she worked. Sequel. A thing that follows. She looked at her join again, at the inner join she'd written first, which returned only the customers who had orders, and she understood suddenly that the inner join answered a different question than the one being asked. The inner join was about presence. The question on the board was about absence, about the people who existed in one table and left no trace in the other, and to find them you couldn't look for them directly. You had to ask for everything, all the customers including the unmatched ones, and then keep only the rows where the order columns came back empty. The nothing was detectable only as a shape around it. She wrote LEFT JOIN, then IS NULL, and ran it, and six rows came back, and Karlee leaned over without being invited.

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"That's the whole trick."

Karlee copied it, of course, in the way that meant she would take it apart at home until she understood it or didn't, and Kaylee let her, because she remembered being the one leaning, last month, before the sorting unit had rearranged everyone's standing. The lab's windows showed the parking lot and beyond it the fence, and the long grass along the fence undulated in the wind, one wave passing through it and then another, and she watched it for a minute instead of starting the next problem. In their English class they were doing existentialism, and the teacher kept saying that Sartre's point was that existence preceded essence, that you were thrown into the world first and defined after. Kaylee had written in her notes that she didn't see what that had to do with anything. Now she thought about the customers table, about people who existed fully in one place and produced nothing in the other, and about how a database would never ask whether that nothing meant loneliness or freedom or simply an empty order history, and she thought maybe that was the limit of the tool, or maybe it was the limit of her, and she couldn't tell which, and she was honest enough with herself to leave the question open.

Ms. Chan came down the row and paused at her screen. "Six," she said. "Correct." Then she moved on to Trevor, who had eight rows and a look of private defeat, and Kaylee turned back to the blank file for the next exercise, Customers and Payments this time, and began to type.

Karlee was still watching the grass move. "Do you think it's sequel or S-Q-L?" she asked.

Kaylee's fingers stopped above the keys. She thought about fossils, about sounds that outlive their spellings, about questions you answer with what's missing. "I think it's both," she said, "depending on who you're talking to," and she hit Enter and ran the query.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
The gown came in a plastic sleeve that smelled like someone else's storage, and Maya couldn't get the zipper of it to sit straight on her shoulders while she stood between parked cars in the lot behind the gym. Her mother leaned against the Honda taking photographs, and Ms. Das was wandering the rows of cars in her own doctoral robes, saying something to each graduate she passed like a benediction or a dare. Maya held her cap down against the wind and looked for Gia.

Gia had texted that she would come, which surprised Maya, because Gia had left school in junior year and mostly avoided anything with the word graduation in it. But there she was by the chain-link at the far end, out of dress code as always, work shirt from the distribution center, hair tied up with a rubber band she had probably gotten off a bundle of asparagus. Maya crossed the lot with her gown dragging on the asphalt.

"You look like a judge," Gia said.

"I look like a traffic cone." Maya laughed and then didn't, because Gia's eyes had a scraped-out look, and under it, something stubborn. "You came."

"I came to tell you something before you disappear to your fancy school with your munificent scholarship." Gia said the word the way she said most words now, half bitter and half showing off, and it was munificent, the letter Maya had gotten in March, enough money that her mother had cried over the kitchen table. "I've been applying everywhere for eight months. Eight months. Grocery, warehouse, front desk, everything."

Maya's first instinct was to say it would happen eventually, and she stopped herself, because Gia would hear the lie in it like a dropped coin on concrete. "What did they say?"

Gia pulled her phone from her pocket and scrolled to a note she had written, which Maya understood was her whole defense prepared in advance. "I looked it up. In 2023, unemployment was 3.9 percent for workers 25 and over with a high school diploma. Without one, 5.6 percent." She let the numbers sit there in the wind. "I keep thinking, almost four percent, that's nothing, that's other people. Then I remember which side of it I'm on."

"Two points," Maya said slowly, and she found herself turning the numbers over the way she did in Ms. Das's statistics elective, the one elective Gia had mocked her for taking. "It's only two points apart. And it's 25 and over, so it's not even about people like us yet. There's time." She wasn't sure whether she was arguing for Gia or for herself, or whether the numbers meant it was a small gap or an unbridgeable one, and she said so. "I honestly don't know which way to read that. Both feel true."

"See, that's the thing about you," Gia said, almost fond. "You can hold two ideas in your head and not pick. Out here they make you pick."

Ms. Das arrived then, robes flapping, and pressed a program into Gia's hands and one into Maya's, telling them the ceremony would start late because the podium microphone had died, and that she had to go indemnify the borrowed sound equipment against whatever the jazz band was about to do to it, waving a liability form from the rental company as she hurried off. Gia watched her go and said, "She still uses words like that on purpose."

They sat on the hood of the Honda, gowns and work shirts together, and Maya, who had felt all week like a neophyte being escorted into some profession she hadn't earned yet, asked Gia what she wanted, actually wanted, not the job search but the want underneath it. Gia was quiet for a long moment, picking at the rubber band on her wrist.

"There's a shift supervisor spot opening at the center in the fall," Gia said. "They train you. It's real money. I applied Monday." She looked at Maya sideways. "Your mother's taking pictures of us right now, by the way."

Inside the gym, later, while Maya stood in the alphabetized line waiting for her name, her phone buzzed twice. The first was the scholarship office confirming her fall enrollment. The second was Gia: got it. supervisor. start august. Maya read it standing in her gown among two hundred classmates about to receive the diplomas that statistically mattered by two points, and typed back congratulations, and then deleted it, and typed instead, can I list you as a reference?

Gia's reply came before Maya's name was called. sure. says here they want someone with a high school education. you have that, right?

Maya stepped forward toward the podium, laughing, with the phone still lit in her hand.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers.
story:
The library's third floor smelled of warm dust and old carpet, and Nevaeh had claimed the corner carrel by the window because it was the only one with an outlet that worked. Her laptop was open to the scholarship application, cursor blinking after her name. The essay prompt wanted five hundred words on a technology issue that mattered to her, and she had written, so far, one sentence. Below her, on the second floor, the new self-checkout machines had replaced the circulation desk where Ms. Lim used to stamp due dates by hand, and every day the line of students moved through them like water through a filter.

Daven dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of printouts and no apology for the noise. "You're doing the Ferrell scholarship too?" he asked, tapping her screen. She tilted it away from him, a reflex she noticed only after she'd done it.

"Trying. I can't pick a topic. Everything sounds like a Wikipedia article."

"Write about the cameras," Daven said. "They put new ones in the stairwells. My mom works custodial here nights, and now they count how long she stops on each floor." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, and that lightness was what made her uneasy. She looked at the ceiling corner behind him, at the small black hemisphere she had never once thought about.

Tyrell arrived twelve minutes late with a paper bag of vending machine chips and the particular energy of someone who had been arguing in his head the whole walk over. "It's nothing," he said, before anyone had asked him anything. "All of it. The cameras, the data, whatever. I've got nothing to hide."

Nevaeh had heard this before, from him, from her uncle, from half the internet, and it had always sounded like a truism to her, so obvious it barely needed saying. Today, with the cursor still blinking, she found she wanted to test it. "Would you mind a list of everyone you call?" she asked. "Just a list. Numbers and how long you talked."

Tyrell chewed. "It's just phone records. Metadata, not even the words."

"That happened," Daven said, flipping through his printouts, and Nevaeh realized he had been researching the same territory, that they had been circling the same thing without knowing it. "In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, like numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers." He slid one page across the table. Tyrell picked it up, and his chewing slowed.

Nevaeh watched him read it, and the room felt quieter than it was, the hum of the HVAC suddenly audible. She was thinking that his answer, "nothing to hide," was almost tautological, that it proved itself by assuming what it wanted to prove, that privacy only mattered for guilty people. But she was also thinking of the self-checkout machines downstairs, of how Ms. Lim had been reassigned to shelving, of how automation and surveillance were not the same thing and yet kept arriving together, wearing the same reasonable face. She didn't want to write an essay that treated them as one monster. She wanted to be fair, and fairness was slower than outrage.

"Okay," Tyrell said finally. He put the page down and squared its edges against the table, twice. "Okay, but I still didn't do anything wrong, so who cares who knows I called my grandmother for forty minutes on a Tuesday?"

"You called your grandmother for forty minutes on a Tuesday," Nevaeh said, "and now I know you were sad, or broke, or in trouble with your mom, and I can guess which by who else you called that week. Nobody needs the words." She heard her own voice go flat and precise, her mother's voice, and she stopped. It augured badly for the essay, this certainty, because certainty was what she distrusted in other people. She softened it: "I don't know where the line is. I just know 'nothing to hide' doesn't tell us where it is."

Tyrell looked at the ceiling hemisphere, then at the window, then back at his chips. Downstairs, a machine chirped its small mechanical chirp, and somewhere a gate alarm went off and was silenced. Daven pulled out a pen and wrote something in the margin of his printout, shielding it with his hand the way Nevaeh had shielded her screen, and she thought: that gesture, that tiny reflex, was the whole essay, if she could only write it honestly. She turned back to her keyboard and typed the second sentence.

Then Tyrell said, quietly, not looking at either of them, "The calls were to a crisis line. In March." He folded the printout in half. "Nobody knew that but me and them."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
story:
Alexander spread the photocopies across his grandfather's dining table, weighting the curling pages with salt shakers because the window was open and the October air kept lifting the corners. His grandfather's house smelled of coffee and old newsprint, and the radio in the kitchen murmured a baseball game no one was watching. On Saturday he would argue that the Soviet Union bore the chief responsibility for the Cold War, a position he had drawn at random and defended, so far, with the confidence of someone who had read exactly one book.

The one book had been William Appleman Williams, or at least the parts of Williams his class handout quoted: American economic expansion, the open door, a country that could not tolerate a closed sphere. Alexander had underlined the quotations twice. But Jaelyn, who would argue the opposing side, had sent him a photograph of her own notes with the caption, you're going to get destroyed, and Alaina, who had judged last month's debate, had told him his case sounded parochial, like America was the only country with motives that year. He had resented the word until he looked it up and found it fit.

He had come here because his grandfather kept a shelf of history books nobody was allowed to throw out, and because at home his little brother had claimed the kitchen table for a science project involving three kinds of mold. His grandfather came in carrying two mugs, set one down beside a salt shaker, and read over Alexander's shoulder without touching anything.

"You're taking sides," his grandfather said.

"I have to. That's the assignment."

His grandfather drank his coffee and went back to the armchair by the window. He offered nothing further, which Alexander had learned, over seventeen years of visits, was the old man's way of offering everything.

He found the book almost by accident, wedged between a biography of Truman and a water-stained atlas: John Lewis Gaddis, The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947, published in 1972. He turned to the argument and read a page, then another, and the salt shakers stopped mattering. Gaddis, as far as Alexander could tell, refused to hand down a single verdict. Neither side, the book argued, could bear sole responsibility. Alexander sat back. His whole case was built on the claim that one side could, and did.

He remembered then a Saturday in seventh grade, the two of them at this same table, when his grandfather had tried to show him how to read the wind before casting a fishing line off the dock. Alexander had insisted the flag on the boathouse was enough, one direction, simple, and his grandfather had said nothing and let the line drift slack while a gust from the west, invisible behind the trees, pushed his bobber somewhere Alexander hadn't predicted. He had been furious about the fish. He had not, until this moment, thought about the lesson.

He called Jaelyn, and she picked up on the second ring with the sound of her own pages shuffling behind her voice.

"Did you know there's a whole position where nobody's to blame alone?" he said. "There's this book from 1972, by Gaddis, The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941 to 1947. He argued neither side could bear sole responsibility for the whole thing."

"What's that called?" Jaelyn asked. He could hear her pen clicking.

"Post-revisionism," he said. "It's called post-revisionism."

There was a pause, and then a laugh that was more surprise than mockery. "So we've both been sharpening knives for a fight the sources won't referee."

They stayed on the phone for an hour, walking each other through what they had, and somewhere in the second half of the hour Alexander changed his mind, not about the facts but about the shape of Saturday. He would still argue his assigned side, but he would concede the joint responsibility where the evidence pressed, and the concession would not be a retreat; it would be the thing that made his remaining claims worth hearing. Jaelyn said she might do the same, and Alaina, texted for a ruling, replied that judges could tell the difference between someone arguing a position and someone who had earned one. He wasn't sure that was true of every judge. He wasn't sure it was true of him yet, either. The discernment to know which evidence to press and which to let breathe felt like something he was borrowing rather than owning, and he tried to say so out loud, to the room, and found he had no listener.

His grandfather was asleep in the armchair, the game still murmuring, the late light coming through the window and lying across the open book in a bar that made half the page glow and half of it dark. Alexander took his phone out and photographed the book lying there, the title legible, the argument inside it holding two weights at once, and sent it to Jaelyn with no caption. Then he gathered the salt shakers and stacked the photocopies, and set the thinnest one, the Gaddis, on top.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
story:
Mr. Otieno slid the outline back across the desk and tapped the margin where he had written "one thing at a time?" in red pen. Cole had organized his historiographical essay in decades, first the Romantic historians, then the Marxists, then the revisionists, and the problem, apparently, was that every paragraph ended with "but then everything changed," which Mr. Otieno said was not an argument but a shrug.

"You have two weeks," Mr. Otieno said. "The question isn't who was right. The question is what they were arguing about."

Cole took the outline to the library at lunch and sat across from Frances, who was highlighting a biology diagram with the concentration of someone defusing a bomb. He spread his notes between them anyway. He had quotations from three historians and a page of dates, and no idea how any of it held together. Frances looked up once, said "that's a lot of paper," and went back to the mitochondria.

The breakthrough came from Keven, of all people, in study hall the next morning. Keven had checked out a stack of books out of stubbornness, having decided in September that he would be an autodidact on the French Revolution whether the course required it or not. He pushed one across the table, a fat paperback with a cracked spine. "Lefebvre," he said. "He wrote it in 1939. It got translated as The Coming of the French Revolution. That's the one Mr. Otieno keeps calling the orthodox view."

Cole read the first chapter while Keven played a game on his phone under the desk. Somewhere in the middle of a section on the countryside, he stopped and read a passage twice. Lefebvre hadn't treated 1789 as one event at all. He had described it as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular, and peasant. Cole copied the four into the margin of his notebook and underlined them, then sat looking at them long enough that Keven glanced over.

"What."

"Nothing. It's just." Cole turned his notebook so Keven could see. "It's four things happening at once. Aristocrats against the crown, the bourgeoisie, the people in Paris, the peasants. All in the same year." He had been trying to line the historians up in a row when the thing they were arguing about wasn't a row. The later writers weren't simply correcting the earlier ones; they were picking up different revolutions out of the pile and holding them to the light. A paragraph could move by revolution instead of by decade, and each school's disagreement would show up inside it instead of being shunted into the next section.

He spent that evening drafting. The paragraph on the bourgeois revolution was easy, almost too easy, because everyone had an opinion about the bourgeoisie and Cole had more quotations than he could use. The peasant revolution was harder; the historians he'd read barely looked at the peasants, and he wasn't sure yet whether that silence was his own research problem or theirs. He wrote the paragraph anyway and left a question mark in the margin beside it, which felt like cheating and also like honesty.

On Friday he showed Mr. Otieno the new outline, braced for another red pen. Mr. Otieno read it through without speaking, which was either a good sign or the opposite. "Whose idea, the structure?"

"Mine," Cole said, and then, because Keven was within earshot and had gone peevish about credit before, he added, "Lefebvre's, technically. I borrowed his four revolutions and used them as sections."

"That's allowed," Mr. Otieno said. "That's what the word means." He wrote something at the top of the page and handed it back. It said "better," which was not a grade and not praise, exactly, but Cole folded the outline and put it in his pocket instead of his binder.

Frances found him after last period at the picnic table behind the gym, still revising the paragraph on the peasants, crossing out a sentence and resuscitating it in different words two lines lower. She set her bag down and looked over his shoulder.

"You said this was boring," she said.

"It is," Cole said. "Mostly." He turned the notebook toward her and pointed at the list in the margin: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular, peasant. "Four revolutions, one year. Nineteen thirty-nine, this guy Lefebvre. Everything after him is people arguing about which one mattered." Frances sat down, unwrapped a granola bar, and said, "Which one mattered?"

Cole capped his pen. "I don't know yet. Ask me Monday."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
The argument started over the flyers, which was how most arguments in Mr. Hall's old classroom started, even though Mr. Hall had retired in June and Ms. Crowchild had taken his place. Someone had taped a voter registration poster to the whiteboard, and Celine had peeled it off, folded it in half, and dropped it in the recycling bin before the bell.

"You can't just throw that away," Ella said. She fished it out and smoothed the crease with the heel of her hand.

"It's decoration," Celine said. "It's a school pretending to care. My cousin voted last time and it changed exactly nothing, so why perform?"

Mylee, who was sitting on the radiator with her boots tucked under her, looked up from her phone. "That's not even true, statistically. CIRCLE, that research center at Tufts, estimated that fifty percent of Americans aged eighteen to twenty-nine voted in the last presidential election. Half of us. And you think it changed nothing? Half showing up moved numbers all over the country."

"Half showing up means half didn't," Celine said. "That's the point."

The bell rang, and Ms. Crowchild closed the door, but the argument didn't close with it. It migrated into the discussion about the school board election, which was the actual lesson, and then into a detour about apportionment, how the district lines had been redrawn so that their neighborhoods were split between two board seats, diluting their votes the way water dilutes juice. Ella took notes, but her notes drifted. She had turned eighteen in September. The election was in three weeks. She had a registration form folded in the front pocket of her backpack, filled out but not mailed, and she had been carrying it there so long that the paper had gone soft as cloth.

After class, Ms. Crowchild stopped her at the door. Not to lecture. She asked whether Ella had eaten, because Ella had looked pale during third period, and when Ella admitted she'd skipped breakfast, Ms. Crowchild produced a granola bar from her desk drawer, the kind with chocolate chips, and pressed it into her hand. "You can vote on the school board race," she said. "The people who decide what money goes to which schools. Your sister's school, actually." Then she let Ella go, having said nothing more, which was her way.

Ella walked home through the crepuscular stretch of late afternoon, when the streetlights had come on but the sky hadn't given up. Her sister went to the elementary school across the highway, the one with the trailers instead of classrooms. Ella's father worked nights and voted only when someone reminded him; her mother had never registered in this state. In her family, voting was treated like flossing, something a person intended to do. Ella had absorbed that, and she had also absorbed Celine's bitterness, and she had absorbed Mylee's statistics, and she noticed that she had never actually assembled any of it into something she herself believed.

That night she texted Mylee. Can you send me that Tufts thing? Mylee sent the link, and Ella read it twice at her desk while her mother watched television downstairs. Fifty percent of young people voting, and Mylee arguing that this mattered, and Celine arguing that the missing fifty percent proved futility. Both of them, Ella realized, were using the same number as a weapon in opposite directions. The number itself was silent. It didn't say whether half was a triumph or an indictment, and neither girl had asked what the other needed to hear.

She thought about Celine's cousin, whose vote had changed nothing, which was technically true of almost every individual vote ever cast. And she thought about Mylee, who did the reading and showed up and wanted company in showing up. And she thought about the granola bar in her pocket, half eaten, and how Ms. Crowchild had noticed her before saying a word about civics. There was a version of caring that started with the person and a version that started with the cause, and Ella suspected they were supposed to meet somewhere, and she couldn't yet say where.

The next morning she found Celine at her locker. "I'm not going to argue with you," Ella said. "But I mailed my form yesterday. If you want, we could go together on election day. Not to convince you. Just so you don't have to stand in line alone if you decide to." Celine shut her locker and looked at her for a long moment, thumbing the dial without spinning it. "You don't think it's pointless?" she asked. "I think your cousin's vote didn't do what she wanted, and I think that's a real thing," Ella said. "And I think half of us showing up is a real thing too. I'm going anyway."

Celine didn't say yes. She said, "What time do the polls open," and turned and walked toward homeroom, and Ella stood there holding her backpack strap, the folded, mailed registration form's ghost still pressed against the pocket where it used to be.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
Brayden spread the graph across his grandfather's kitchen table, smoothing the crease where it had folded in his backpack for three days. The line at the bottom crawled sideways for half the century, then bent upward like a hand rising out of water. He had printed it after school because his grandfather's house was the one place with no wifi and no distractions, only the hum of the refrigerator and the smell of coffee gone cold in the pot.

"You're doing homework at my table on a Saturday," his grandfather said, setting down two mugs. "That's a first."

"It's not homework exactly." Brayden turned the graph toward him. "Mr. Haile wants me to explain this to the astronomy club on Tuesday. How carbon dioxide traps heat, and how to read this. Kallie was supposed to do it with me but she's at her cousin's, so I'm the one who has to stand up there and not sound like an idiot."

His grandfather pulled out a chair. "Then explain it to me. I'm a harder audience than a room of teenagers."

Brayden took a breath. Sunlight comes in, he said, and the Earth warms up and radiates heat back out, and certain gases in the air absorb some of that outgoing heat and send part of it down again, so the planet stays warmer than it would with a bare sky. He traced the graph's flat stretch with his finger, the decades when the numbers barely moved, then the climb after 1950, steeper and steeper, the last point higher than every point before it. His grandfather listened without interrupting, which was somehow worse than being interrupted.

"Here's the part I always get," his grandfather said at last. "How do they know? You're showing me a line going up. Machines didn't measure all this a hundred years ago."

"That's the thing." Brayden pulled out his phone, remembering he'd saved a screenshot before leaving home. "Ace asked the same question when we went to the planetarium talk last month. He thought it was all just computer models, that nobody knew anything before satellites. But the presenter said no, and Ace looked it up right there in his seat." He found the page and read it aloud. "In 1896, a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled."

"Nineteen century," his grandfather said. "Before my father was born."

Brayden nodded. He didn't understand all of it himself, how a man with pencils and paper could reach a number like that a hundred years before anyone put a graph on a kitchen table. But it had changed something for him. Before the planetarium, the whole thing had felt like an argument between channels, one side shouting gloom and the other shouting hoax, and he had assumed the truth was whatever you already believed. Kallie believed one thing, Ace's uncle believed another, and Brayden had drifted between them. Now he held a fact that neither of them had mentioned, older than all the shouting, and it belonged to no channel. He wasn't sure yet what to build on it, only that it was load-bearing.

"You've got a face like a man doing math in his head," his grandfather said.

"I'm trying to figure out what I actually think. Ace keeps sending me these videos, and some of them sound smart, and then I look one up and it's, I don't know, specious. It sounds right until you check it. Like one guy said the graph is fake because one station in Hawaii sits near a volcano. I checked. The stations don't agree because of a volcano, they agree with each other all over the planet." He tapped the table. "But I also don't want to be the guy who just believes whatever comes from the side I like. That's the same problem pointing the other direction."

His grandfather turned his mug in a slow circle. "When I practiced medicine, epidemiology was the discipline of tracking where an illness moved and why. You didn't take one patient's story and call it the pattern. You took the whole map." He glanced at the graph. "Your line there. It's a map, isn't it. Many stations, many decades, one shape."

Brayden looked at the rising curve and felt something settle, not a conclusion exactly, but a footing. He could stand in front of the club and say what the measurements showed, and say what stayed uncertain to him, and refuse both the people who promised doom by Friday and the ones who promised nothing was happening at all. The honesty of the first calculation, done by hand in 1896 by a man who never saw a computer, was the kind of thing that could still enthrall him, the way some kids were enthralled by sports stats. Maybe that was enough to start with.

On Tuesday he stood at the front of the room with the graph projected behind him, Kallie in the second row giving him a small thumbs up. "This line is a hundred and some years of air, measured," he began. "And people have been calculating what carbon dioxide does since before my grandfather's father was born. Arrhenius, 1896. He figured out how much the Earth would warm if CO2 in the atmosphere doubled, with paper and pencils." He picked up the marker and walked to the board, and drew a sun, and an arrow coming down, and an arrow trying to leave.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
Nicole found the bookshop on the Thursday before her last week of high school, when she was supposed to be returning a library book and instead stood in the doorway smelling dust and paper while rain ticked against the window behind her. The summer reading club met in the back, past the shelf of Remainders, four chairs pulled into a rough circle around a stack of overturned crates. Kamille was already there with her annotated copy of Jane Eyre, and Julian sat with his feet on a crate, which Mr. Iyer, the shop's owner, pretended not to notice.

The problem had arrived by text that morning. "I finished the feminist lens notes," Kamille had written, "but Mr. Iyer wants us to try the Marxist one too, and I don't get how you hold both at once without one eating the other. Bertha Mason is locked in an attic because she's a woman, or because she's colonial money gone wrong, or both, and I can't tell which reading the passage actually supports. Bring your brain Thursday." Nicole had read the message four times on the bus, then again in the queue at the bank, where her mother was arguing about the word insolvency with a teller who kept apologizing. Nicole had thought: that word belongs in this somehow.

Mr. Iyer opened the session by reading aloud from a slim pamphlet he kept behind the counter, a copy so old its cover had gone the color of weak tea. "The history of all hitherto existing society," he read, "is the history of class struggles. That's how the Communist Manifesto of 1848 begins its first section. Marx and Engels. Now, does it fit what we read?" He set the pamphlet on a crate where everyone could see it, like a stone put down in the middle of the circle.

"That's too big," Julian said immediately. "One sentence about all of society can't say anything about one governess."

"It can if the governess is the point where the classes touch," Nicole said, and heard her own voice surprise her. She opened her copy to the passage she'd marked, the scene where Jane first tours Thornfield Hall and Mrs. Fairfax explains the household's rhythms. She read aloud the lines about wages and station, then laid her palm flat on the page. "Okay, so the feminist reading first. Jane keeps saying she wants to be more than a governess, that she has a mind, that being poor and plain and little doesn't make her less of a person. That's her refusing the box that her sex circumscribes her with. That's real. Mrs. Fairfax isn't locked in an attic and she's still stuck."

Kamille leaned forward. "But then apply the other lens to the same page. Jane's anger isn't only about being a woman. It's about being paid. She can't leave Thornfield because leaving means hunger. Her freedom is exactly the size of her wages."

"Which is the class struggle," Julian said slowly, pointing at the pamphlet. "Right there in one governess's morning."

"It's both, and they're not the same thing, that's what's getting me," Nicole said. "When Rochester calls her an equal, he's lifting her up as a woman, as a spirit, and he can do that precisely because he owns the house she stands in. The equality is real in one frame and a kind of gift in the other. A gift can be taken back." Kamille wrote something in her margin. Julian took his feet off the crate.

Mr. Iyer asked whether Nicole thought the two lenses could be ranked, one truer than the other. She turned the pamphlet toward herself and read the sentence again, silently this time, the history of all hitherto existing society. "I don't think I can rank them yet," she said. "The Marxist reading explains the money moving underneath the marriage plot. The feminist reading explains why Jane minds. I can hold both if I admit I don't know which one is doing the real work in any given line. Maybe that's the skill. Or maybe that's a failure and I'll find out in college."

"It's not a failure," Kamille said. "Write it down like that. 'I don't know which lens is doing the real work.' Half our class would kill for a sentence that honest."

Mr. Iyer closed the session by handing Nicole the pamphlet. "Return it when you've finished your first semester," he said. "I want a report." She walked home through the last of the rain with the pamphlet in her jacket pocket, Jane Eyre under her arm, and when she passed the bank she stopped and looked at the windows for a long moment, thinking about wages and rooms and the slow, glacial way ideas seemed to move through a whole society before anyone felt them. Then she texted Kamille: "Thornfield is a bank with a garden." Kamille replied with a single row of question marks, and Nicole started typing the paragraph she would read out loud next Thursday.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: An overvote happens when a voter marks more choices than a contest allows, and that vote is not counted for that contest.
story:
The cursor blinked over the second bubble, and Kayla told herself she was only admiring it. She had filled in one oval for mayor with the mouse, a clean digital mark, and then hovered over a second oval because the second candidate also seemed, in some inchoate way, like a person who might not be terrible. Her grandmother had voted in every election since arriving with forty dollars and a sewing machine, and her mother voted when she remembered, and Kayla had spent the whole drive to register saying she would be different, deliberate, the kind of voter who read things. She had, in fact, read things. She had read so many things that both candidates now seemed equally plausible and equally slippery.
