The house was quiet. Her mother was at the late shift, which meant Kayla had the laptop and the kitchen table and the whole weight of civic adulthood to herself. Official ballot, one choice for mayor, the screen said. She had already voted for the school board, feeling virtuous about it, and had typed her answers to the ballot questions with the seriousness of a person taking a medical exam. Mayor was the last contest. She clicked the second oval.

The screen went grey in a small, precise way. Overvote detected, it said. This contest allows one choice. If you mark more choices than the contest allows, your vote will not be counted for this contest.

She sat back. Not counted. Not counted for this contest, the whole office, the whole thing she had driven to the library to register for in August when it was ninety degrees and the volunteer had said congratulations like she'd won something. All those months of calling herself a voter, and she had nearly voided her own ballot by liking two people at once, which, if she was honest, was how she had chosen most things in her life, including Mariah, including Blair, including her second-choice college.

She called Mariah first because Mariah would know the word. Mariah worked at the polls, had been trained, came home with lanyards and opinions. "It's called an overvote," Mariah said, around something she was eating. "You marked more choices than it allows. So it doesn't count for that contest. Did you actually do it?"

"No," Kayla said, which was technically about the final submission and not about the click, which she had undone with a frantic backspace. "I almost did it. There's a warning."

"There's a warning on the machine. On paper there isn't. Some guy today filled in two circles for county judge and then argued with me for ten minutes about his intentions." Mariah swallowed. "Intentions don't get scanned."

Kayla thanked her and hung up and sat with her hand on the trackpad. She thought about the guy at Mariah's polling place, whoever he was, two dark circles and a sincere face, believing he had expressed something rich and double-hearted. There was a version of herself, the one she'd been at sixteen, who would have found that romantic. Look at me, unable to choose, so full of considerations. That girl had wanted very badly to be a virtuoso of nuance, and the ballot, it turned out, had no category for nuance. It had a category for one oval.

She opened a second tab and did what she had sworn not to do, which was look at the candidates again. She had promised herself, loudly, at Blair's birthday dinner, that she would decide before Election Day and then not look at anything. She had told this to Blair, who had said, "So you're voting for the first person you read about, basically," and Kayla had not spoken to her for the length of one slice of cake. But Blair, being Blair, had a point that was annoying precisely because it was small and true: deciding early wasn't the same as deciding well. It was just deciding fast with better manners.

She read for forty minutes. One candidate had said a thing about the community college that Kayla's mother would have found insulting and Kayla found merely vague. The other candidate had a record on the transit board that could be read two ways, and she read it two ways, and then she caught herself preparing to admire the ambiguity like it was a symptom of sophistication. The ballot had already told her what it thought of that. Mark more than it allows, and you get nothing.

She thought about Ms. Brennan, junior year, who had told the class that the hardest essays were the ones where you had to actually pick a side, and that most of them would spend their lives constructing careful sentences to avoid doing it. Kayla had written in the margin of her notebook, at seventeen, avoiding commitment is its own commitment, and had been extremely pleased with herself. It had not, as far as she could remember, ever resulted in her committing to anything.

She moved the cursor. She filled in one oval, the first one, not because she had achieved certainty but because she had run out of honest ways to stay neutral, and neutral, she now understood, was not a place you could stand on a ballot. It was a blank. She submitted, and the confirmation screen came up with its cheerful little checkmark, and she sat there in her mother's kitchen with the refrigerator humming.

She texted Blair: voted, no thanks to you. Then she made toast, because adulthood apparently included toast at ten p.m., and ate it standing up, looking at the dark window where her reflection and the yard existed at the same time, both of them equally there, only one of them counted.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Ryder filled out the application at a corner table at Meridian Coffee, where he had been nursing the same small drip for an hour because the manager had told him to wait. Elisabeth slid into the chair across from him with her own cup, foamed milk in the shape of a tulip, and asked what he was doing.

"Job interview. Sort of. She said come by after four and we'd talk." He turned his phone face down on the table so she couldn't see how often he'd checked the time.

"You're nervous," Elisabeth said. "You've rearranged the sugar caddy twice."

He had, though he hadn't noticed. The little paper tubes kept sliding out of alignment like they wanted to escape the tray. He admitted he wanted the job more than he'd let on at school, where everyone treated working as either a joke or an inevitability, depending on whose parents did what.

"My mom keeps calling it 'the real world,'" he said. "Which is a dysphemism, honestly, because the real world is also chemistry class and this coffee shop and the bus. It's all real. She just means the part where money happens."

Elisabeth laughed, then leaned in with actual news: Joelle had gotten hired at a bakery just across the state line, twenty minutes away, and had texted a photo of her offer letter that morning. Ryder read the number twice. It was more per hour than Meridian paid, and Meridian was the nicer place, the busier place, the one with the line out the door on Saturdays. It made no sense to him, and the unfairness of it felt almost physical, a stone he kept turning over.

The manager, a woman in her forties with flour or chalk dust on one sleeve, came out from behind the counter at four ten and sat down without ceremony. She asked him the usual things, then said the rate plainly, and he, because he was seventeen and incapable of letting a wrong number stand, asked why it was less than the bakery's.

"Federal minimum's been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009," she said, and shrugged, palms up, as if presenting a fact she hadn't chosen. "States and cities can set higher. Ours hasn't. Joelle's bakery is in the next state over." She let that sit, then added that everyone started at the same number here and that tips on weekends made a difference, and asked if he wanted the Saturday and Sunday shifts.

He said yes before he had finished deciding, and she went back behind the counter with his paperwork, and Elisabeth raised her tulip cup in a small toast. He tried to hold two thoughts at once, which was harder than it looked. One thought was that the law itself was a floor, not a ceiling, a number so old it predated everything he could remember about his own life, and that calling this "the market" hid a choice someone had made. The other thought was that complaining was easy and showing up was the actual thing, and that the manager hadn't invented the number any more than he had. Both seemed true. Neither dissolved the other.

When Joelle arrived after her shift, still smelling of bread, she slid into Elisabeth's chair, kicked her apron under the table, and demanded details. Ryder told her what he'd be earning and watched her face do the thing his had done.

"That's it? That's legal?" she said.

"It's legal. Whether it's fair is a different question," Ryder said, and found he believed it, both halves. She asked whether he'd take it anyway, and he said he'd take it, work the weekends, and keep the question. It felt like less than an answer and more than nothing, a down payment.

He pulled the sugar caddy toward himself and squared the paper tubes one last time, deliberately now, so they sat straight. Behind the counter, the espresso machine hissed, and the milk in the pitcher began to coagulate at the edges where it had sat too long, and the manager called over the grinder's noise, "You start Saturday. Seven a.m. Sharp."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
Mackenzie had the study saved as a screenshot, and she read it once more in the car while her mother found a parking space. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. She had found it at two in the morning, half researching for Mr. Horváth's class and half thinking about Dean, who had asked her to bowl on Thursday and then said "or Friday, whatever's easier" in a way she had replayed four times. A 1999 study. She knew it was ridiculous to build an evening on something older than she was, but she locked her phone anyway and went in.

The alley smelled like floor wax and rented shoes. Mr. Horváth stood at the counter in his league shirt, arguing with the cashier about lane twelve. "It eats left turns," he was saying. "Every ball drifts. I've bowled here nineteen years, I know what a dead board is." Nola was already there, waving from the bench, because Nola had insisted on coming, since a first date at a bowling alley was, in her words, objectively funny and she intended to watch. Her own want was simpler and she announced it: she needed to break one-forty before Saturday's league qualifying, and her shoulder was behaving, and tonight was practice.

Dean arrived on time, which she catalogued. He got shoes in a size that made him walk like a duck, and when he caught her noticing he said, "Don't prognosticate about my form. I'm going to be terrible and I want that stated up front." She laughed before she meant to. First frame, he rolled a gutter ball and then another, and she beat him badly without trying, and something in her unclenched. Maybe the study was irrelevant. Maybe she could just be here.

Then she caught herself doing it. When he leaned an elbow on the ball return, chin in hand, she leaned an elbow on the ball return, chin in hand, four seconds late, and she had to fake reaching for her drink to make it look natural. When he crossed his ankles waiting for his ball, she crossed hers. She was doing the mimicking. The study said the liked one was the mimickee, the person being copied, not the copier, and the partner wasn't supposed to notice the mimicry, and she was neither the right person nor unnoticed, because Nola was watching her with narrowed eyes.

"What are you doing," Nola said, quietly, while Dean was at the snack counter.

"Nothing."

"You're mirroring him like a yoga instructor. Stop. He's going to think you're mocking him."

"He won't notice."

"I noticed in one frame. You're my best friend and you looked like a waxwork of yourself."

Mackenzie's plan collapsed at lane level. Somewhere between the third frame and the fifth, though, it reversed on her. Dean rolled a strike and did a small, private fist pump, and a frame later she rolled a strike and did the same fist pump without thinking, and he grinned at her like they'd invented something. Later, when she leaned forward on her knees watching his ball, she saw in the glossy reflection of the lane that he had leaned forward on his knees too. She hadn't done anything. He was copying her posture now, or they had both arrived at the same lean, and she couldn't tell which, and the study gave her no way to tell which, and that was the part no screenshot covered.

"See," Nola said during the seventh, back from her practice frames, flexing her shoulder, "this is why I don't date. Too much wondering. I hit pins, pins fall down. Clean system." She rolled her practice ball on lane eleven, a beautiful hook, and cursed virulently at lane twelve when Mr. Horváth's next shot drifted wide for no reason anyone could prove. Mr. Horváth pointed at the lane like a prosecutor. "Witness," he announced to the whole alley. "Sixteen witnesses." The cashier shrugged without looking up.

In the eighth frame Mackenzie stopped performing the study and just sat with the not knowing. He liked her or he liked the company or he liked the coincidence of two people whose elbows happened to match, and the Chartrand and Bargh result was real, it was measured, people liked partners more when the partners mimicked, even when the people never noticed being mimicked, and still it couldn't tell her what this specific boy felt in this specific smoky room. She could hold both things. The science was true and it was not an answer.

"I have to ask," Dean said, as they traded shoes back at the counter. "Frame four. You did my exact fist pump."

"That was mine first. You did it frame three."

"Frame three was improvised. Frame four was theft."

"Then I owe you a soda."

He paid for the sodas before she could reach her bag, and they stood by the door while Nola finished her qualifying practice, one-forty-two on her last game, shouting a wordless victory at the ceiling. Outside it had started to rain, and Mackenzie's mother's car wasn't there yet, and neither was his ride, so they stood under the awning and he matched her posture, elbow on the rail, or she matched his, and neither of them said which.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, such as late payments, can be reported for seven years, and bankruptcies for up to ten.
story:
Camille had circled the economics table twice before she let herself stop in front of it, the way you might circle a dog you weren't sure about. The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and coffee, and banners from a dozen departments hung above folding tables staffed by students who all seemed taller than she was. She was here, technically, to accompany her brother, a senior, though she'd spent most of the morning pretending that wasn't true.

She'd come because of a fight, more precisely. Not a shouting kind. The quiet kind, conducted over text, with her friend Sawyer. Three weeks ago Sawyer had shrugged off a missed payment on his first credit card, the one he'd gotten the day he turned eighteen, and when Camille had asked whether that mattered, he'd typed back a single sentence: "It's like twenty dollars, it'll fade." She hadn't known enough to argue. That not-knowing had bothered her more than the argument itself, the way a word you can't quite recall bothers you all afternoon. So when the university's open house flyer mentioned a personal finance session in the economics wing, she'd folded it into her pocket like evidence.

The session was held in a lecture hall with seats that rose in curved tiers, and most of the people scattered through them were parents. Camille sat in the back row beside a girl with purple headphones around her neck, who introduced herself as Elliot and said she was here "for the free pen and to escape my mom." A student at the front, a senior giving the talk for some financial literacy club, was taking questions, and a father near the front had just asked something about a relative's bankruptcy.

The student's answer arrived before Camille had finished unwrapping her pen. Most negative information on a credit report, like late payments, could be reported for seven years, she said, and bankruptcies for up to ten. She said it plainly, the way you'd say the distance to a rest stop, and moved on to the next question, but Camille wrote the numbers down twice, once in her notebook and once on her hand, because she didn't fully trust the notebook.

She looked at the numbers. Seven years. She tried to hold it against something. Sawyer would be twenty-five when the late payment left his report, assuming it had even been reported, which was another thing she didn't know. Twenty-five was an apartment application away, a car loan away, a whole life she couldn't picture for him because he currently couldn't picture it for himself. And yet the student hadn't said a missed payment ruined you. She'd said it could be reported. Reported, Camille noticed, was a softer word than destroyed, though not soft enough to rest on.

The talk ended and the crowd drained toward the refreshment table, and Elliot, who had been quiet the whole time, turned to her. "Did that freak you out too?" she asked. "My cousin did the bankruptcy thing at thirty and he says it follows him like weather."

"Seven years for the other stuff," Camille said, checking her hand. "Ten for that."

"Ten." Elliot whistled. "I was going to get a card this summer just because the booth guy was nice."

"Nice booth guys," Camille said, "are probably not a decision-making framework." Elliot laughed, and they walked out together into the corridor, where the economics department had hung posters of alumni in suits above a display of native prairie grasses the grounds crew had replanted, a small patch of something autochthonous growing under fluorescent light between the vending machines. Camille found herself staring at it. The grass had been here before the building, before the banners, before any of the decisions the posters celebrated, and it would keep doing its slow work regardless.

Later, near the admissions tent on the quad, she ran into Sawyer himself, who was there with his own school's group and who greeted her by stealing the pen from behind her ear. She told him what she'd learned, keeping it to the numbers, not dressing it up as a lecture because she knew how that would land. "So it doesn't fade in a month," she said. "Late payments, seven years. Bankruptcies, up to ten. That's what they can report."

Sawyer turned the pen over in his fingers. For a second she thought he'd deflect, and she braced for it, already drafting her retreat. Instead he said, "Huh," and then, quieter, "I thought it was like a parking ticket." He'd been picturing a fine, something paid and finished, sealed off from the future the way childhood is supposedly sealed off. Now he was recalibrating, and she watched him do it, his thumb worrying the pen's clip. She felt her own position shifting too, less certain than it had been in the lecture hall. She'd walked in thinking the fact was a warning, a set of chains; standing here, she thought it might be closer to the prairie grass, something with a timescale humans hadn't designed, neither cruel nor kind, just longer than a shrug.

"I might call them," Sawyer said. "The card people. Set up autopay or something."

"That doesn't sound like the worst idea you've ever had."

"It's not even in the top ten." He handed back her pen, and behind them a tour group surged past toward the library, a guide's voice promising that this building, that quad, those doors would shape the next four years, and Camille wondered, not unhappily, what shape seven years would make, or ten, and whether anyone standing in this crowd would recognize themselves at the far end of it.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone.
story:
The community center gym smelled of rubber mats and old popcorn, and Christopher had decided, by the second week of January, that winter conditioning was invented by someone who hated teenagers specifically. The coach had them pushing a weighted sled across the basketball court in groups of five, and on Thursday he stopped the drill, put his whistle in his pocket, and said the whole team together pushed like they were moving furniture for a friend they didn't like.

"Individually you're animals," the coach said. "Together you're houseplants. Why is that?"

Nobody answered. Savanah was lying flat on the court pretending to inspect the ceiling for leaks. Natalia, who was only at the community center because her mother taught the pottery class down the hall and the ride home wasn't until five, was doing her homework on the bleachers and not even pretending to care about sleds.

Christopher did care, though not about the sled. He cared about the fact that he couldn't make the numbers line up. Alone, he'd pushed the sled twenty-two feet before his legs gave out. In the group of five, they'd barely beaten that, and it made no sense to him. Five of him should equal a hundred and ten feet. He kept turning it over while he stacked the mats, and at the water fountain he turned it over again, and finally he sat down next to Natalia and asked her, as the resident smart person, whether math was broken.

"Math is fine," Natalia said. "People are the problem. There's a whole thing about it. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, published a study in 1913. He had people pull on a rope, and in a group each person pulled less hard than they did alone."

"That's a real thing? It has a name?"

"Social loafing. I read it for psych." She went back to her worksheet, then looked up. "Why, is your coach maligning the team's effort? He was yelling at Andre for slacking."

"Everybody slacks. That's the point. Even me, probably, and I'm the one doing math about it." Christopher looked at the court, where Savanah was now pushing the empty sled alone, showing off, grunting theatrically. "So it's not that we're lazy. It's that being in a group makes everyone ease off, even when they think they're trying."

"I said I read it, not that I'd solve your life," Natalia said. "Also, Savanah's going to hurt himself."

Savanah did not hurt himself, but he did push the loaded sled alone, wobbling, eighteen feet, which was less than Christopher's twenty-two and which Christopher mentioned, in the spirit of scientific inquiry, roughly nine times on the walk to the vending machines. Savanah bought two bags of chips and called Christopher an epicure of other people's failures, which Christopher had to admit was pretty good, since he did savor it.

At the next practice, Christopher asked the coach if they could try something. They ran the sled drill with a twist: each pusher got a strip of tape on the floor marking their individual start, and after every run the coach called out the distance so they could each track their own number, not the team's. The coach agreed mostly, Christopher suspected, because it meant he could stand still and drink coffee. The first round was ordinary. The second round, when Savanah realized Natalia, who had wandered down from the bleachers and been handed a stopwatch, was calling out his splits, was better. By the third round the whole group was beating their solo numbers, howling every time, and the coach lowered his coffee and said, "Huh."

"It's not that hard," Christopher explained afterward, sitting on the sled like an armchair while the others packed up. "If we can each see our own effort, the group thing stops eating it. We're not five guys sharing one job. We're five guys with five jobs that happen to be touching."

"That's almost wise," Savanah said. "Say it again but worse."

That Saturday there was a cleanup at the riparian trail behind the center, the one along the creek, and the whole team got roped into it as penance for something the juniors had done at the last away game. They hauled brush in pairs and, without anyone proposing it, the pairs started calling out their pile counts to each other, keeping individual tallies, competing. Christopher carried branches alone along the creek for a while, thinking that he still couldn't say where Ringelmann's effect ended and ordinary laziness began, or how much of their improvement was tape on the floor versus just wanting to beat Savanah. He'd hold both ideas at once and see.

He was still holding them when he came back to the truck for the last load and found Savanah, Natalia, and two juniors standing around a pile of branches that was exactly one armful short of complete, all four of them waiting, each assuming someone else would get it.

"I'll do it," Christopher said, "alone, at maximum effort," and went and got the branches.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
Hudson had spread a lawn chair across the flattest patch of grass, a clipboard on his knees, because the kitchen table had been annexed for his mother's paperwork and the porch steps were already taken by Sean, who was eating a popsicle as though the afternoon had no obligations. The clipboard held seven empty boxes drawn in pencil, one for each day, and above them Hudson had written SEASON in block letters, then crossed it out, then written it smaller. The coach had told them at the end of tryouts that making the team was the easy part; the ones who lasted were the ones who could plan a week. Hudson had nodded along with everyone else and then understood, walking home, that he had no idea how.

"You're doing homework in July," Sean said, pointing the popsicle stick at him.

"It's not homework." Hudson turned the clipboard so Sean could see. "It's a training week. Coach wants one from every sophomore who made varsity. Rest days, warm-ups, the whole thing." He had tried a draft on Sunday night: running every day, hard, because the logic of more seemed unassailable. His shins had excoriated him for it by Wednesday, a hot grinding ache that made stairs a negotiation, and he had spent Thursday icing them and being lectured by his father about tendons, which his father pronounced wrong.

Amira came through the gate carrying her own binder, because Amira did everything three weeks early and made it look accidental. She dropped onto the grass, cross-legged, and pulled a printout from the front pocket. "Ms. Janssen gave me this," she said. "I asked her about the training thing because she used to coach. She sponsors the fitness club, did you know that?"

"She gave you the answer?"

"She gave me a chapter." Amira slid it across the grass. "She said nobody plans a season all at once. You cut it up."

Sean leaned over Hudson's shoulder as he read. There was a word in the second paragraph that none of them had seen before, and Amira tapped it with one finger. "It's called a microcycle," she said. "The smallest one. Usually about a week." The chapter laid it out plainly: a whole season divided into cycles, and inside those, the week, the small repeating unit you could actually hold in your hand. Hudson looked at his seven empty boxes and felt the odd relief of a thing he'd already built being given a name.

"So the week is the real project," he said slowly. "The season is just weeks stacked up." He began filling boxes, and this was where the two ways of thinking in his head started arguing. His old self, the Sunday-night self, believed rest was a furlough from work, a temporary mercy granted to the lazy. The chapter, and Ms. Janssen through it, treated rest as part of the work itself, a box like any other box, planned with the same attention. He wrote Monday: easy run, warm-up drills. Tuesday: hills. Wednesday: REST, and then, feeling like a fraud, underlined it.

"You're going to actually not run that day?" Sean asked.

"I don't know." And he was honest about that part, because the pencil could say rest and his legs could still go out the door; that part stayed uncertain, a gap between the plan and the person. "Wednesday I'll find out." He added warm-ups to every box, ten minutes, ankles and hips, the boring insurance his shins had billed him for. Amira read his week upside down from the grass and moved one hard day away from the weekend game, saying his legs would still be full of Friday if he stacked them, and he let her, because she was right and because she had noticed he was favoring his left shin even sitting down.

The light had gone long and amber across the fence, and Sean's popsicle stick lay in the grass like a tiny fallen fence post. Hudson copied the week into his phone, then recopied it onto a fresh page, this time drawing eight weeks behind it, a ladder of little cycles climbing toward September, each one different, each one still just seven days he could survive one at a time. Amira gathered her binder and paused at the gate.

"Tell Ms. Janssen on Monday," she said. "She'll want to know somebody used it."

Hudson looked at the underlined REST and then at the lawn chair's shadow, which had stretched all the way to the tomato stakes without his noticing. "I'll tell her the shin part too," he said. "She should get the whole microcycle."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, both women's hearts are exposed, and a single blood vessel connects them, winding through their hands and hearts.
story:
Simon had promised Ms. Kowalski a written critique by Monday, and the only thing he had produced so far was the word "composition" written twice in his notebook, then crossed out once. The assignment was formal analysis: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings dressed up as arguments. He stood now in front of The Two Fridas with his sketchbook open on his forearm, trying to draw the figures as shapes first, the way she had shown them with the Cezanne print in class.

It was Morgane's fault he was here at all. She had texted him a photograph of the gallery ticket stub with the caption "homework you can't fake," and Rayhan had added a thumbs up, and now the three of them were arranged across the bench like birds on a wire, all of them sketching badly. Rayhan kept drawing the hearts as cartoon valentines until Morgane elbowed him.

"Draw the red line," she said. "The one that goes between them."

Simon looked again. He had assumed, from the postcard-sized reproduction in the textbook, that the blood was simply spilling, that the exposed hearts bled down the white dress as a general atmosphere of injury. But the actual painting was more precise than that. Both women's hearts were exposed, visible through the opened space of their clothing, and a single blood vessel ran from one heart to the other. It wound through their joined hands, thin and then thick, and back into the second chest. He traced it with his pencil on his own sketch, and the line went crooked because his hand was unsteady.

"One line," he said. "I thought it was two. Like, each one bleeding separately."

"It's one vessel," Morgane said, not looking up. "Connecting both of them."

He sat with that. In his draft critique, written last night at eleven o'clock, he had argued that the doubled figure represented a self divided against itself, two identities staring in opposite directions, one in Tehuana dress holding a portrait of someone absent and one in European clothes holding nothing at all, with a small pair of scissors. That was symbolism, technically. But it had skipped the painting itself, skipped the storm-grey sky, the flat horizon that seemed to presage something without saying what, the way the seated figures made a near-symmetrical composition that never quite closed. Ms. Kowalski had written "look longer" at the bottom of his last essay, and he had resented it for a week before admitting she was right.

It had not been happenstance that put him in her class. He had chosen art appreciation because it fit the gap before lunch, and for the first month he had treated it as a rest period. Then, during a unit on portraits, he had found himself explaining to Rayhan why a Rembrandt self-portrait felt like an accusation, and the explanation had come out organized, almost mathematical, and he had liked the sound of his own thinking for the first time in that building. He wondered whether the choosing had been as careless as he claimed, or whether he had seen something in the course description and pretended not to.

The colour he could now actually name. The white of the left Frida's dress was cold, slightly blue in the shadows, while the Tehuana dress carried warm reds and golds, so that the palette itself split the two women the way the composition did. Yet the single vessel crossed the divide. Simon tried to hold both observations at once, the division and the connection, and found they did not cancel out. The symmetry was a structure, and the vessel was a structure, and a critique that described only one of them would be half a painting.

He thought of his cousin, who had moved back from the capital last spring and who everyone described as having become a different person there, as if a person could shed one self and grow another. His cousin used the word phenotypic once, talking about moths in industrial cities, how the visible trait changed with the environment while something underneath stayed what it was. Simon had filed the word away as interesting and useless. Standing here, he was less sure it was useless. He did not know how to put any of that into a formal analysis, and he did not know whether he should want to. Ms. Kowalski had forbidden biography. She had not forbidden thinking, though the line between them kept moving under his feet.

"She's not looking at us," Rayhan said, pointing with his pencil. "Both of them are looking out. Like we're the ones being judged."

Simon wrote in the margin of his sketch: one vessel, two hearts, joined hands. Then, underneath: the connection is the composition. He underlined nothing, because he was not sure yet which part he would defend on Monday and which part he would revise at the bus stop, scribbling on the back of his hand. Morgane leaned over and read the margin.

"That's actually good," she said.

"Maybe," said Simon, and turned back to the painting.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the second line of the staff, marking that line as the G above middle C.
story:
Peyton had promised herself she would finish the sixteen bars before Friday, and by Wednesday afternoon the promise had decayed into four bars of melody and a page of crossed-out chords. She stayed after the last bell in the music room, where the radiator clanked and the upright piano held its tuning only in the middle register. Ms. Hernández had left the manuscript paper in a stack by the metronome, and Peyton spread it out across two chairs, weighting the corners with valve oil and someone's abandoned reed.

The melody itself she trusted. It moved the way she wanted, up a sixth at the second bar, then settling, and the chord changes underneath had stopped fighting it after three drafts. What she did not trust was the notation. Writing music by hand was like copying a language she could speak but not spell, every stem and flag a chance to lie about what she meant.

Leanna came in with her viola case and a bag of chips, and sat on the piano bench without asking. "Play it again," she said, mouth full. Peyton played the four bars. Leanna listened with her eyes shut, which Peyton had learned was a compliment. "The last bit. Play it higher."

"It can't go higher, it's already up there."

"Write it down and I'll read it. I want to try it against the chords." Leanna was faster at reading than at trusting Peyton's descriptions, so Peyton copied the melody onto a fresh staff, careful with the beams, careful with the accidentals. Leanna took the page to the stand, set her bow, and played.

It came out wrong. Not badly, which would have been fine, but wrongly, everything a third too low, the melody sitting in the mud of the viola's lower strings. Leanna stopped and squinted at the page. "Is this what you meant? Because this is not what you played."

Peyton came over and looked. The notes were right. The rhythms were right. She had even gotten the F sharp marked. Then she saw it, the clef at the start of the line, drawn with its curl swooping down around the bottom line instead of the second. Jayde, who had drifted in halfway through, leaned over Peyton's shoulder and read the look on her face. "You drew it wrong," she said. "That's why everything shifted."

"The curl goes around the second line," Peyton said slowly, tracing it with her finger. "That's the whole point of it. The second line is where the G lives, the G above middle C. That's why they call it the G clef. It's not a decoration. It's a landmark." She felt slightly ill thinking of all the times she had drawn the symbol as flourish, as ornament, never once asking what it was for. Her mother called this ionizing a subject, rendering it into noble gas, untouchable; Peyton had done it to notation for years, treating the staff as scenery rather than a map.

She took the page back, recopied it with the curl circling the second line, and handed it over without comment. Leanna played it again, and this time the melody lifted exactly where it was supposed to, the sixth climbing out clean over the chords. "There," Leanna said. "That's the thing." Jayde had pulled out her phone to record and Peyton almost told her to stop, because until ten minutes ago she had believed that recording work-in-progress was a kind of complicity in her own half-effort, an agreement to settle. Now she nodded instead. "Send it to me," she said. "I want to hear it when I'm not guarding it."

Ms. Hernández looked in at the door on her way out, listened for one bar, and said only, "Lock up when you go." She did not offer notes, which Peyton understood as its own message. Peyton sat back down at the piano and pulled the manuscript toward her. The question of whether the twelve unwritten bars would resolve or modulate was still open, still genuinely uncertain, and she found she preferred it that way, the way a problem is better than a wound. She picked up the pencil, set the point on the second line of the empty staff, and drew the curl around it first, before anything else.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
story:
The mailbox at the end of Cole's driveway had a door that stuck, so that checking it felt like prying something open rather than receiving it. He checked it anyway, twice on Saturdays, once on school days, and there was never anything for him except the electric bill and flyers for gutter cleaning. The letter, when it came, would be thick or thin. Everyone said that. A thick envelope meant welcome; a thin one meant a single page and a careful paragraph of regret.

His father had mailed the application for him in December, because Cole had stood at this same mailbox for ten minutes with the fat envelope in his hand, unable to let it go. It had gone out with two stamps and a return address written in Cole's smallest handwriting, as though the whole thing might still be taken back. Since then he had learned the rhythms of the postal service the way other people learned weather. He knew the truck came at 2:40. He knew which substitute driver slammed the box and which one left the flag up.

The application itself had been less terrible than he'd feared, and he had Julianna to thank for that, or possibly to blame. She was a year ahead, already a freshman in spirit if not yet in body, and she had sat at his kitchen table in October with her laptop open, half amused and half contemptuous. "You know there's a thing called the Common Application," she said. "One application, and you send it to a bunch of schools instead of writing twenty separate ones." She told him it had started in 1975 with fifteen member colleges and now had more than a thousand, and she said it with the air of someone revealing that fire had been invented. "I would have died without it," she said. "Actually died." Cole had nodded and felt, briefly, cheated of a suffering he'd been promised, some rite of endurance that would have proved something. Instead the form took an evening, and the essay took three, and the whole thing slid out of his hands easier than it should have.

Scarlet had a different theory about all of it. She sat behind him in Ms. Farah-Ali's class, and she had watched him check his phone for portal updates with such frequency that she finally leaned over her desk and said, "You know it doesn't come faster if you stare at it." She believed in letting things arrive in their own time, a philosophy she applied to grades, to relationships, to the boreal winter that had settled over their town in November and refused to lift, and which she claimed to find beautiful in its way. "Everything's just sitting under the snow," she said once on the walk home, "waiting. That's not the same as nothing happening." Cole had argued with her then, a little, because waiting felt to him like the opposite of living, a kind of ennui with better manners. But he had thought about it since, on the days when the mailbox produced nothing.

Today was a Wednesday, cold enough that the metal lid bit his fingers. The truck had come and gone, and when he forced the door open there was one envelope inside, white, with the college's return address in the corner, his name printed in a font that looked almost like handwriting. It was neither thick nor thin. It was exactly medium, which no folklore had prepared him for.

He stood there without opening it. He thought about his father driving to the post office in December with the envelope riding on the passenger seat, and about Julianna at her own mailbox in another town, waiting for her own answer, and about how one form had gone to so many places at once and would come back to him as several separate futures, each one calling itself the real one. Scarlet would say to open it standing right there, in the cold, on the terms the day offered. Julianna would say to sit down first, open it near food and witnesses. Both of them were probably right in some proportion he couldn't calculate.

He turned the envelope over twice. Then he put it inside his jacket, against his chest, and walked back up the driveway without opening it, holding it there with one flat hand.
